The Premiums received during the year in the industrial Branch were £2,911,295, being an inerease of 2116.773. The claims of tue year amounted to £1.123.4 The number of deaths was 135,861. SUMMARY OF THE QUINQUENNIAL REPORT. FOR THE PERIOD ENDING 318 T DECEMBER, 1886. In the Ordinary Breech the Annual Premium income has Increased from £l4l 731 to 2407.340. The ass trance Fund has grown from 2144,783 to £1,764,600. In the Industrie: Branch the Annual Premium Income has Increased from .t 2,05 1,024 t • 23.065 M. The Assurasise Fund has grown f rom £1 721,493 to 24,937,003. The Total Assets of the Company have grown from £2,580,002 to 26.811,954, being an Increase of £4,231,952 in the five years under inspection The rate of expladiture during the Qulncruennium in the Ordinary Branch has remained nearly stationary, at little more than teu per cent. A reduc- tion of seven and a-half per cent, haa been effected in the ex- penses of the Industrial Bi emit. It will be seen from ltf.. Dewey's Report that the average ,1 duration of all the Policies in the Industrial Branch is now no less than five end a-halt years, a satisfactory indication of the success which is attending the eff irts of the Directors to in- crease the duration ot the assurances. EXTRACT FROM MR. A. H BAILEY'S REPOP T. Having :rim time to time bee, consulted as to the princi- ples upon which the valuations sla old be made of the out- standing liabilities of your company on the list Do ember lest, I have now exAmined the results of those valuations, the pro- cesses employed in obtaining and checking the partictears from I the records, and the r-ethods adopted to In. ore accuracy In the calculatims. dame notion may be formed of the magnitude of the work when it is stated that the number of assurances in f .roe, ex- clusive of annuity grants is 7.196,917; so th .t if each policy were on a different life, which is probably not very far from the truth. this lives of 19 it per cent, or vim y nearly one-fifth of the entire popnletion of Gloat Britain and Ireland, are assured in this company. The business is carried on under two distinct branches, the " Ordinary " and the •. Industrial" In the former, the pre- miums are payable annually, half-yearly, or quarterly; and the terms and conditions resemble those of the unejorlty of the Life Assarauce C,onmanies of the eonntry. In the latter branch the rates are higher, became, without exception, the premiums are payable weetly, an arrangement which the ordinary companies 'will not adopt on account of the heavy ex- pense and .trouble of collect In. but which experience seems to show is the only wa whereby the wage-earning portion of the community can be reached. For ten years the two B anckes have been conducted bade. prmdently of each other, as if they were distinct saleties ; separate arenunts being kept, and separate investments made for each. Being now, however, Dractlcaly worked by the same agents. the public select whichever best suits their con- venience, and comeqen ly the distinction between the char- acter of the business of the two branches is becoming less. As an instance of this it is noticeable that while the average amount assured by each policy in the " Ordinary " Manch bas diminished since the last saluatlon, being now £ll6 against the 2137 five years ago ; in the Or (Mistrial Branch the average amount kris slightly increased, and is nhw 29 Bs, ORDINARY BRANOW—The groeth of this Branch has been very remarkable. The premium income from the assaraiices Is £406,862, having nearly trebled in the quinquenr 'um, and being surpassed by only four other Life Assurance Companies in the United Kingdom. The basis upon which the valuation of the liabilities has been made is explained in Mr. Hughes' report. It may be shortly described as follows —The past experience of Assured and Annuitant lives has been adopted for the rates of mortality ; 3 per cent for the rate of int, re,t ; and 221 per cent of the memium income. which is the whole of what is called the load ng, has been reserved for future ex- penses, profits, and cintiugencles. Of the ample sufficiency of this reserve no doubt cart be entertained, especially as it has now been re olved that the whole expenses of this Branch shall be limited to 10 per cent of the premiim income, INDUSTRIAL BRANCH —ln this Branch the Premium Inc,ime has now reached the enormous total. of £3,065,551, payab.e in weekly premiums averaging ab.-ut twopence each. The ages of the lives assured vary fram 1 year to upwards of 100, four- teen centenarians being found open the registers. The females out-number the males In the proportion of 1.076 to 1,000 an excess a imewhat above that of the general populist ion,whereas In the ordinary companies lb. number of male lives assured is found to be about eight times that of the females. A large number of the policies in force have been effected on the lives . of children. And, if death occur during the first year of as- surance. the contract provides that, with some exceptions, a deduction shall be made from them= assured. From these circumstances some modificatious in the prtnel. pies of valuation adopted for the Ordinary Branch bee ime necessary. These are explained by Mr. Dewey in his report, with which I concur. For instance, the table of mortality employed for the Ordinary Branch represents the experience of adult male lives only, children being altogether omitted. For the Industrial Branch. the,efore, Farr's English Life tables have been used, and separate valuations mscle for the male and female risks, the mortality of the two sexes being different. Again the rate of mortality of children, unlike that of adults, diminishes fri.m year to year up to a certain age. And there- fore the risks on lives of children not exceeding ten years of age, and those under all Policies granted during last year, have been treated as short term assurances, for which a nomi- nalleserve only is necessary With these exception.' a valua- tion on the same principles as in the Ordinary Branch has been made of all the outstanding Policies. These facts and figures speak for themselves, and it is hardly necessary to add how eminently satisfactory the results of this elaborate investigation must be to ail who are interested in the welfare of the Company. EXTRACT FROM THE EXPORT OF MR. W. HUGHES, ACTUARY OF

TEE ORDINARY BRAN. The Valuation is as before on the net premium system, the whole of the loading or differs ze between the premiums pay- able and the risk premiums being served as a provision for future expenses and profit. 'lbis loading amounts to £91,078 per annum. The number of Policies In force at 31st Decemter last was 85.089, assuming with Bonus £10,226,238, and prodlc• ing an annual premium income of £407 360 8s Of this amount £13,726 is reassured at an annual cost of £6OB Is. A feature worthy of note is the large proportion of Endow- ment Assurances lately effected. At the last Valuation, 1881, ticese Policies formed 16 per eent, of the whole number in force ; on the 31st December, 1886, there were 31.120 of these Policies, being no less than 86 per cent, of the whole number of assurances. The net results of the Valuation are as follows: Life Assur- ance Fund, 31st December, 1886, £1,764,600; Reserve for Life Assurance and Annuity Contracts, £,457, 878. P.ETRACT FROM THE REPORT OF MR. div.head: Xottri.
div.p: Xottri.

AN IPTY NEST. A grave old Nan and a maiden fair Walked together at early morn: The thrushes up in the clear cool air Sang to the-farmer planting his cora. And, oh, how sweet was the fresh-turned mould! And, oh, how fair were the budding trees! For-daisy's:silver and daffodil's gold - Were full of the happy honey bees. "Ah, look, there's an empty nest," she said, "In-clrveonder where sing the last year's birds?' Then'the old man, quickly raised his head, Though scarcely he noted her musing words; He tore the nest from the swaying tree He flung to the winds its moss and hay,'- And said: "When an empty nest you see, Be sure that you throw it far away." -"But why?" she asked, with a sorrowing face— ".Why may not the pretty home abide ?" Because," he answered, "'twill be a place In which the worm and the slug will hide. 'Last year 'twas fair enough in its way— It was full of love and merry with song; But days that are gone must not spoil to-day, Nor dead joys do the living joys wrong." The maiden heard,with a thoughtful face— • Her first false love bad gone far away— And she thought, Is my heart become a place 1 For anger and grief and hate to stay? Down, heart, with thy sad, forsaken nest! Fling far thy selfish and idle pain; •- The love that is ours is always the best: And she went with a smile to her work again. —Mary A. Barr, in Harper's Magazine.

Question for father—Father, with much solemnity: "Whatever you do, my bey, begin at the bottom and work up." Son, deferentially: "Bat father, suppose I was going to dig await ?" A very precise person, remarking upon Shakespeare's line, "the steiod men do is often inMrred with their bones," carefully observes that this interment can generally take plasm without crowding the bones. To the true girl in all her relationm--as daughter, sister, friend—in all her actions, in all her words, faith- fulness will he the first consideration. Faith is the root of all good works, and it is a fruitful parent of all other graces. Her , word must be her bond through life. A true girl will not make a promise and break it, nor say one thing and mean another, but will be true in word and deed. A learned professme in the course of a long climb to the summit of a Highland mountain, took the trouble to enlighten the gille by whom he was accompanied regarding the electric light, the telephone, and other modern inventions. As Donald never condescended to give the slightest indication of either interest or wonder, the professor expressed his surprise at his silence, on which the Highlander confidently informed him that he was "a big leaf (liar) himser r It is told of a gentleman that he had a passion for the purchase of second-hand furniture at nuctions, and that in makie-gee good bargains" he had filled his house with antiquated and almost useless articles. Upon one occa- sion his wife took the responsibility, without consulting or apprising her husband, to have a portion cf the least useful removed to an aucsion-room, Great was her dismay when, on the evening of the day of sale, the majority of the articles came back to the house. The husband had stumbled into the auction-room, and not knowing his own furniture, had purchesed it at a better bargain than at first. The foliowing interesting conversation occurred be- tween an attorney and a witness in a case in which a certain tree played a prominent part—Lawyer: "Did you see the tree near the road-side ?" V itness • Yes, sir, I saw it very plainly." Lawyer: "It was very conspicu- ous then?" Witness: "Well, I can't say that, I saw the tree very plainly, though." Lawyer: Well, Well, now, I would like to know why, if it was plain, it wasn't con- spicuous. What is the difference between plain and con- spicuous? Answer that, will you?" Well," replied the Witness, "It is this—l come into this court-room and glance over the bar. I see you plainly among the other lawyers, although you aint a bit conspicuous.' When. Garrick was beginning his career, his great rival was Quin. Garrick was bright and natural, Quin was formal and pompous. It was evident that the death-struggle between the old and the new school was about, to begin. At last it was decided that they should appeal definitely to the public. "The Fair Penitent" was chosen. Garrick performed Lothario _And Quin Horatio. The first act took up a full hour, for the house was full of the advocates of both schools, and both were loud jri their plaudits. At last a trivial and ridiculous, but, as all must have felt, a significant, circumstance, gave Garrick the victory. In the last scene of the second act, Lothario challenges Horatio: "Two hours ere noon to-morrow I expect thee." Quin, with his usual pompous stateliness, paused so long before he gave an answer that some simple fellow in the gallery, really excited by the position, cried out, "Confound you, you coward, why don't you toll the little gentleman whether you'll meet him or not." REVENGE.—But if man has been curbed by hie inanimate surroundings, he, as the most powerful of all organised beings, and, in individuals, perhaps the most numerous of the higher animals, is rapidly reversing the process. He has changed the entire aspect ef vast con- tinents; he has hewn down primeval forests and con- verted their sites into corn fields. To graze his flocks and herds he has exterminated the wild animals which from time immemorial pastured the prairies; and, in several instances, in order to gratify his appetite, he has decreed or is decreeing the death of several gigantic mammals and large birds, which until he burst in upon their haunts were plentiful. Within less than a century, man has drained lakes and joined seas; in the course of his history he has turned gardens into deserts, and made the desert bloom with verdure; he has covered the sites of wigwams with-great cities; and again by his ferocity has so thoroughly erased what were for ages the wonders of Pagandom, that it is all but impossible in Christendom to trace the places where once upon a time teeming towns had for ages hummed with life.—" Our Earth and its Story," February. SCOTTISH BEADLES AND THEIR HumotTß.—ln olden times, the serviceable beadle was armed with a small wooden "nob," or mallet, with which he was quietly commissioned to "tap," gently but firmly, the heads -of careless sleepers in church during the sermon. An instance to hand is very amusing, and is not out of fair probability. In the 02 town of Kilberchan, which is aelebrated in Scottish pqetry as the birthplace of Habbie Simpson, the piper and terse maker of the clachan, once lived and preached a reverend original, whose pulpit ministrations were of the old-fashioned, hodden-gray type, being humdrum, and innocent of all spirit-rousing 'eloquence and force. Like many of his clerical brethren, bQ 'was greatly annoyed every Sunday at the sight of several of his parishioners sleeping through the ser- mon.. He was especially angry with Johnny Plane, the village joiner, who dropped off to sleep every Sun- day afternoon simultaneously with the formal -de- livery of the text. Jelinny had been "touched" by the old beadle's mallet on several occasions, but only in a gentle 'though persausive manner. At last, one day, the minister, provoked beyond endurance at the sight of the joiner soundly asleep, lost his temper. Johnny Plane !" cried the reverend gentleman, stop- 'ping his discourse, and eyeing the culprit severely," are ye really sleeping already:, and me no half through with the first head ?" The joiner, easy man, was quite obli- vious to things mundane, and noticed not the rebuke. "Andre," resumed the minister, addressing the beadle, and relapsing into informal Done, "gang round to the west loft [west gallery} and rap up Johnny Plane. Gie the lazy loon a guid stiff rap on the heid—he deserves et." Round and up to the "west loft" the old-fashebned beadle goes, and reaching the somnolent parishioner, he rather smartly "raps" him on his bald head. Instantly, there was on the part of Johnny a sudden start-up, and between hire and the worthy beadle it hot, under-breath bandying of words. Silence restored, the reverend gen- tleman proceeded with his sermon as if nothing unusual had occurred. After sermon, Andra met the minister in the vestry, who at once made impliryas to the "words" he had had with Johnny in the gallery. But the beadle was reticent and uncommunicative on tho matter, and would not be questioned as to the reception the joiner had given his salutary summons. "Well, Andra," at . lengthesaid the reverend gentleman,." I'll tell ye what; we must not be beaten in this matter; if the loon sleeps next Sunday during sermon, jist you gang up and rap him back to reason. It 's a knock wi' some force in 't the chiM wants, mind that, and spare not." Deed no, sir," was the beadle's canny reply. "I 'll no disturb him, sleepin' waukine for some weeks to come. He threatens to knock pew-bibles and hymn-books out re me if I again deur to *rap' him atween this and Martinmas. If , Johnny's to be kept frae sleepin, minister, ye maim just , pit the force into yer sermon." The following bit of true Scotch humour may be classed in the same category as ' the preceding sketch, the witty impeachment once more coming froth the lips of the minister's own beadle. The story is put down to the credit of the very learned Dr. Macknight, one of the lights of the Scottish Church in his day. The doctor's beadle, or • man in attendance," seems to have possessed a keen sense of dry, pawky *humour, and had judg the doctor's habit of writing and publishing learned Scriptural books as just so much waste of time. "Is the worthy doctor at home asked a reverend caller at the manse one forenoon. "Na, indeed, he is not," promptly replied the beadle. "lie's awa like a chased hare to Edinburgh on a fell fUiliSh job." (The learned doctor had just gone off to the printers with his laborious and erudite work, "The Har- mony of the Four Gospels.") The caller was inquisitive, and on being furthered questioned as to what this " fell fuilish" job might be which so engaged his minister's attention, the witty beadle made answer, "He's gene awe to male four men agree who never cast not" edis- mgreed).—Chambers's Journal.. for roiath, red, or cnimped skin there is nothing equal to t•Beethainta filyeerirre mid Cucumber." div.head: CURIOUS PROPERTY DISPUTE AT
div.p: CURIOUS PROPERTY DISPUTE AT
NEWTON.

In the Lancashire Chancery Court on Tuesday, at Bt. George's all, Liverpool; before Vice- Chancellor Briatowe, the case of °Toenail v. Briawn, an action to Set 'aside or to rectify a deed of *assignment Made by the R4intiff to the defendant was heard. Mr. Neville, M.P., and Mr. Hughes were counsel for the plaintiff, and Mr. Rotch and Mr. Arkle represented the def en- dant.—Mr. Neville said the plaintiff, John Greene% was a retiredinnkeeper, living at Haydock, -and the defendant, lohn Brown, was the nephew of the plaintiff, carrying on the business of a painter and builder in Newton-le-Willows. Plaintiff had reached the age of seventy-five years, and in 1861 be took a 999 years' lease of land situated at Newton, on which he erected a row of six houses. calling them Havelock-terrace. At that period and for some years following be was en terms of friendship with the defendant, who also went by the name of Pierpoint, and who advised him in his affairs. Defen- dant had built the houses, and pressed plaintiff to continue building, but the latter was unwilling to do so on his own account, and in July, 1884, ex-cuted what he thought was a sub-lease of the remainder of his land to the defendant, in order that Brown might build on his own account. De- fendant afterwards built a further six houses on the land. It now appeared that the deed was an absolute assignment of the whole of the property to the defendant in considera- tion of plaintiff's "natural • love and affection." This was quite contrary to Greenall's intentions. life bad explainer' to the defendant dhat he proposed to do about the sub- lease, and remarked that his lawyer had said a deed would be necessary. After this conversation plaintiff and defen- dant went to the office of a Mr. Wilson, solicitor, Wigan, I where a deed was produced already prepared, and this, after it had been read over, was signe 1 by Greenall, who had perfect confidence in the (Intendant. This was the deed et assignment, but plaintiff being deaf coeld make nothing out of the contents of the document. The defendant had promised previously to have the deed execwed by a Mr. Ellie, of Wigan, but on arriving at this person's office defendant made an excuse, and took the plaintiff to Mr Wilson. To show what really were plaintiff's intentions it was stated by Mr. Dieetille that his client had eince re- ceived the rents of the Havelock-tmace houses, and the defendant those of the other honest On the Watt, In 1885 the plaintiff made a will, having married a second Ulna, ama- in this document be treated the Havelock-terraCe property as being still his, and left an interest in it to his wife. Al-. though he was in the room at the time the will was read, defehdant did not suggest that the property had been as- signed to him. In the same year defendant advised the plaintilf to make certain alterations In the property, and these the latter instructed him to perform. In consideration of the work defendant sent in a bill for £lOO. Defendant's I explanation of the matter was that the assignment was exe- cwed to save the payment of legacy duty on the plaintiff's death, with a verbal understanding that Greenall was to I have as a life interest the rents of the Havelock-terrace ,houses.—The case was adjourned. The action was resumed on Wednesday, when plaintiff, in 'pros/1.-examination by Mr. Rotch, said he could not under- , stand the deed when it was read over to him at Wigan by 1 Mr. Wilson, the solicitor, because he was bard of hearing. , He denied that he informed any of the tenants that he had assigned the property to the defendant in 1835, or that it it would be the defendant's at his (the plaintiff's) death.— Several witnesses were called in support of the plaintiff's case.—Mr. Rotch said that, far bcyond the value of the Havelock-terrace houses, the defendant's honour was at stake. Evidence would be called on behalf of the defendant to prove that the plaintiff was not in ignorance of the con- tents of the deed, when be signed it, but that be knew per- fectly well what he was doing; that the deed was executed in pursuance of an arrangement that had ,been well con- sidered and thought out; and that the effect of it was ex- plained to him and he aereed to it. After having heard the evidence be did not think it would be possible to hold that the plaintiff was in ignorance of what the nature of the deed was, still less that the defendant, knowing the plaintiff's ignorance, permitted him te sign it. He should press for a decision on the merits of the case.—The case had not con- Eluded when the court again role, /On Thursday, after private c ,nsultation between the par- ties,before the Vice-Chancellor, Mr. Retch stated in court that both parties were indebted to his Honour for the suggestions made, which the plaintiff and defendant un- reservedly accepted, subject to a few alterations each as ' the proportion of rent the defendant ought to pay. Mr. Rotch then read ever the terms of settlement, in which it was stated that all imputations on both sides were to be absolutely and unreservedly withdrawn ; the deed of July, 1884, to be cancelled, and the lease to be delivered to the plaintiff ; tbe deed to be settled by the registrar in case the parties differed, each party to bear and pay his own costs of the action and deed.—The defendant was then sworn, and in reply to Mr. Botch said when he gave instreetions on the 4th July, 1884, for the assignment, and when the assign- ment was executed, he was in the 'honest belief that his uncle intended to assign to hime Havelock-terrace as well as the vacant piece of land.—The Tice Chancellor said it was very creditable to both sides that they had settled the matter entirely—Mr. Rotch said he was obliged. to his Honour for coming in and enabling them to settle the matter cm terms agreeable to both parties.

A punctual man cart always find time, a negligent one never. • When we think of the Future, we do not often think of the Future of Futures. Great opportunities are generally the result of the wise improvement of small ones. Mankind are always happier for having been happy once; the memory of happiness is happiness. "Faithful Ones" should ponder this—A boy described the heathen as "folks wot don't fight over religion." Strive for that serenity of spirit that will enable you to mike the best of things. 'That means contentment in its best sense. A good test of one's condition is ability to LW well. Toil that does not interfere with sleep cannot be said to be excessive. Idleness that prevents sound and refresh- ing sleep, and takes away the keen appetite for it, robs a man of this among other blessings of life, and makes existence empty. Shortly before he died, Sir Walter Scott said, "I have been perhaps the most voluminous author of my day,, and it is a great comfort to me to think that I have tried to unsettle no man's faith, to corrupt no man's principles; and that I have written nothing which on ray death-bed I should like blotted out."

Of all education that has for its object the right fulfilment of parental duties would seem among the most important. Yet, as a general thing, that relation is entered upon with only crude and desultory ideas of the principles involved; and, while intelligence and experience slowly bring a measufee of wisdom, it often comes too late for the most pressing necessities. A great portion of all the worst mischief, negative and positive, that ever afflicted the world is traceable to what Oople erroneously call conscience, but which is Often only a hateful compound of ignorance, prejudice, and vindictiveness.' The duty of man is to improve those faculties which enable him to think and act cor- rectly. He must make his conscience a good enlightened conscienee ; then, and then only, will he be entitled to honour and credit in acting upon it. Like flakes of snow that fall unperceived upon the earth, the seemingly unimportant events of life succeed one another. As the snow. gathers together, so are our habits formed. No single flake that is added to the pile produces a sensible change ; no single action creates, however it may exhibit, a man's character; but as the tempest hurls the avalanche down the mountahiscand overwhelms the inhabitant and his habitation, so passion, acting upon the elements of mischief which pernicious habits have brought together by imperceptible accumu- lation, may overthrow the edifice of truth and virtue. WHY HE DECLINED.—Last winter, having to fulfil a lecturing engagement in a Western city, Mark Twain " boarded " a train that is noted for its slowness and is always avoided by regular travellers. But the Lecturing Committee had written to the humourist agreeing to meet him at the depOt upon the arrival of the train, and so he had no alternative. Two hours' travelling served to ex- haust Mark's patience. Stopping the conductor as he passed through the car, Mark asked as civilly as he could, ''Why don't you people run this train faster?" The conductor, ignorant as to who his questioner was, rejoined, "It runs fast enough to suit us. If you don't like the rate of speed, why don't you get out and walk ?" "Well, I would,' returned Mark, but that some friends won't come to meet me till the train arrives; and I don't want to be waiting around the depot for tyro or three hours."

LAND SUBSIDENCE IN THE SALT DrSTRICTS. at the sixth meeting of the On Tuesdav evening, Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society, held in the lecture-room at the Museum, Mr: Thomam Ward, of Northwich, read an interesting paper on "Land subsidence in the salt districts of Cheshire." Mr. T. J. Mylands occupied the °hair, and there was a good attendance.—Tbe LECTURER said that the salt dis- tricts of Cheshire bad for many years past been noted for very extensive sinkings of the ground, sometimes occurring suddenly, at other times slowly het continuously. The town and district were the most noted for these subsidences, and, beyond an occasional reference to the other districts, he should c.n flue his attention to Northwich, as containing everything necessary to illustrate subsidence in all ita forms. The beds of rock salt in Cheshire lay at the bottom of a great hollow, jar depression. That depression, with various interruptions, extended from the extreme north of Lancashire to the lower porion of the Severn valley, and in the deepest !portions of it beds of salt had been deposited, as at Preeswell, near Fleetwood, at Northwich, Winsford, Lawton, Nantwicb, in west and south Cheshire, and at Droit- wich, in Worcestershire. Doubtless there were a number of salt beds in that extensive area not Vet discovered, as brine bad been found at Warrington, Safford, Shirlevwich, and other planes. After the carboniferous era a great chanee took place in the district ender notice. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON. THURSDAY. • The news of the, freak plot against the life of the Czar has created 644ofound sensation of sympathy. With a considerable and influential section of Lon- doners there is a sort of hereditary distrust and dis- like of Russia. But an act like this of these wretched students' brushes away all prejudice, and Conservatives, equally with Liberals, pity the con- dition of the Czar and his family. The most power- ful potentate in Europe, he must be t4e most miser- able of men. There is not a Cossack in his arniy, a peasant in•kis vast dominions, who would change places vith him. It is enoughto drive a strong man mad to have tb'undergo the daily and hourly restrictions dictated by his position. The Czar of all the Russias is like a man carried about in a cage with a horde of wild beasts sniffing round the cage, ready , for any opportunity to spring upon him and devour him. ... Now that the.•first •• shock of surprise has died away, everyone is asking how the event will influ- ence the. issue of peace'or war. It is feared in some J quarters.that i.n.adesperate attempt to concentrate j attention elsewhere than upon his own person the 1 Czar will precipitate war. It is a Shocking, thing' Mat Such an 'issue Riould lie in the hand of a man ' who can scarcely be expected to be in possession of his full senses. • Yet so it is, and in all the Capitals people are anxiously -waiting the developinent Of events at St:PetersbUrg; 'Elsewhere the war cloud seems to have lifted. Germany and France have apparently resolved to postpone the inevitable struggle. Austria is quiet, and order reigns in Bul- garia. It is only in the north where a. gloomy, morose, and unnerved man is in hiding from a cor- don of would-be 'assassins, that danger lurks. A good deal is said and written about the slow pro- gress of business in the Rouse of Commons. It is slow enough and wearisome enough for those in com- pulsory attendance. But as compared with what used to take place between 1880 and 1885, when the Conservative Party-were in league with the Par- nellites in opposition to Mr. Gladstone's Govern- ment,. we are getting along like a house on firs. There is nothingjike obstruction as it was known in the palmy dais of the Fourth Party. There have been no all-ntglit sittings;' and very few protracted ones. No suspensions of members, and no serious conflicts with the Chair. The Irish members and others including gentlemen 'sitting on the right hand Of the Speaker, have insisted upon their right to discuss so important a matter as the introduction of the Closure. But we have not yet come any- where near the length of time the, discimsion took in the Autumn Session of -1882, when the Closure was opposed tooth and nail by the party who h 3.8 now adopted it as its own. It must not be for- gottenthat of late Committee of Supply has divided the week with - discussion of the New Procedure Rules, and very fair, progress has been made with the votes.

Mr. Gladstone is not very constant in his attend- ance at the House. He generally looks in at ques- tion time, but goes away in good time for dinner, and happily does ,not return. But this abstention from older habit must not be taken as indicative of consciousness of failing strength. He is, in truth, about as well and as lively as he has been any time these five years past. Whilst he is in the House he holds a succession of levees, at which he does most of the talking. On Tuesday night a characteristic little incident befel. Mr. Dillwyn had just moved his amendment to the closure rule. Mr. Gladstone was about to leave the House, but before going der- sired to speak to the member for Swansea. Had ' the late Mr. Disraeli, or the present Lord Harting- ' ton, been animated with a similar desire, they would have "'communicated with Mr. Dillwyn through the-whip, and invited him to visit there on the Front Bench. The juvenile vigour of Mr. Glad- stone could not brook such lengthened procedure. Observing Mr. Dillwyn sitting in a corner seat be- low the gangway, he briskly walked down and seated himself on the steps of the gangway whilst with animated gesture he conferred with the mover of the amendment. There was some ten- dency amongst the Conservatives to snigger; but for the most part the House looked on in silent wonder at the restless activity of this youthful septuagenarian. There is nothing new in the political situation. The Round Table Conference, of which a fortnight ago we heard precise assurances of being on the verge of a happy conclusion, remalni in the posi- tion it was then simaltaneously described im this column. Perhaps, as Mr. Gladstone and his friends remain immovable, Mr. Caine and the Radical sec- tioh of the Dissentients arel more, eager to bring about reconciliation. That will certainly come, but on Mr. Gladstone's terms, not Mr. Chamber- lain's. The United Kingdom will presently be in a par- lous condition. At the 'present moment .it is de- prived of the presence of the Duke of Connaught who is in India, and the Duke of Edinburgh who is in the Mediterranean. On Saturday the Prince of Wales leaves for Berlin, on a somewhat prolonged visit in connection with the celebration of the Em- peror's birthday ; and on Tuesday week the Queen celebrates the real commencement of the London season by setting forth on a holiday visit to the Continent. We have the Duke ,of Cambridge left. But in an unusually marked mariner the comitry will be left alone for a space of time t 3 get on with- out Royalty. The Queen's, Continental visit 'will be prolonged for at least a month. She is going to Cannes in spite of the earthquake, and will stay. there NWeek• Three weeks will be given to Aix- les-Bains; and a.little over a week will' be occupied in making the journey. The Princess Beatrice and Prince Henry of Battenberg accompany. the her Majesty, something I fancy to the relief or Prince, who would rather sem his state of bon- dage anywhere than in Great Britain. Whilst in Scotland he is Obliged to go about in kilts, in which he cuts a- serrY figure by the side of the stalwart natives, and in the home circle at Windsor and the ' Isle of White he is snubbed by his Royal brothers- in-law. The only IaP,P3T time he has is' when by some lucky chance he is detained a niat in London and may g 6 to the theatre. According to the mali- cious reports that, ever pursue. the luckless Prince, there are segildings on the next day: But there are also plea§anYmemories to cherish. , ~.Lore Randolph Churchill • will probably bif much I mortified pp. the perfect regularity with which things in the political and social world go on in i his absence. As far as Government prospects in the House of Coremons are concerned they are cer- tainly the smoother since he is not there. He has inadvertently supplied an opportunity, of showing that he is not mdispensible. This may have a de- sirable effect. He is to be back at the end of the month, and *ill make his appearance in the House before the adjournment for the Easter recess. He is also to speak at a public meeting, where he is expected to make up for lost time. The rumour recently car- rent of negotiations for his return to the Cabinet have entirely dropped. The fact is Lord Ran- dolph is reported to have said—and certainly his relatives and intimate friends say it for him—that he will resume office only as prime Minister. This seems a bold assumption, but it is not nearly so startling as would have been, 18 months ago, the forecast that he would be Chan- cellor of the Exchequer and Leader of the House of Commons. He has got a pretty strong following in the House of Commons, and a very large one in the country. He also profits by being dissociated with the Government in its present stum4ling and tot- tering _condition. The principal obstacle to the realisation of his anticipation is the fact that with a reunited Liberal party the chances of there being a call for a Conservative Premier is exceedingly re- mote.
Public Analysts have submitted CADBURY'S COCOA. ti) MOe. tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining aid nourishing beverage, Beware ni Advt.

div.p: ARCH 19, OF HC

OPITAL ROA Ott In the St. James's Hospital the men's surgical wards are at the top of the building. That is where the.a.cci+ dents are brought in. . . . At about half-pub' six- o'clock onedwinter afternoon the well-known sound came up the tube, and sister Janet directed that one of my beds should receive the new-corner. It was a young man, a strapping fellow. Of his face I coal see little, for it was bound up for injuries to the bead and jaw, and one of his arms was broken. I expected to hear that he had fallen from-a scaffold, or had been run over in the street; but the policeman said they had brought him from his own home, where'they had been told he had fallen down stairs. The story mild only have one meaning, I feared. The majority of the cases come to us through drink; and the policeman, as he told it, made a sign which was sufficiently explanatory, if any explanation were needed. - "There was an old woman mixed up in it—his mother —and I take it they'd been soaking together," said he. The new patient took no part in these explanations. Though he had not uttered a groan, I could see he was in great distress, and he could speak only with difficulty. "I'm glad, at any rate," said I, "that you appear to have no wife and family to be pinched while you're out of work. You're better off than a great many that come here." • He nodded his head and looked at me' and I saw at once that he had been misjudged—he had not been drinking. The look was too direct and intelligent, and so expressive of manly endurance that. my sympathy went out to him at once We have sympathies as tender as other women, we nurses, I hope, though sometimes we joke and laugh, when other *omen would cry. "You're not a drinking man ?" I asked. He shook his head. . "The doctors will tell you to-morrow morning that's in your favour." Hicks, the stout cabman in the next bed, overheard the remark. "Now, nurse, come we ain't no need to be told that. We ain't under no delusion as td the yoos in this here p!ace, and if we wos, 'ere's Thomson at and to expound 'em to us at hany hour of the day her night." This speech was intended as a challenge to Thomson, the pale-faced shoemaker in the next bed, who accepted it as such, and a discussion followed, which was much relished by, such of the invalids round as could hear it. "I'm a redit to my principles," says Hicks, expanding his cheeks. " Fifteen stun if a pound, and roses in my cheeks. A- pretty complexion yours is for the blue ribbing." "I won't deny you're a good weight," chuckled Thomson, "so much the heavier for a fall when you've taken a drop more than enough." v." I ain't ashaitted of a broken leg. , It's a haristocratic complaint," retorts Hicks, "not like your pleurises and such-like that comes of livin' low." I did not hear any more of the discussion, nor which had the best of it in the end. Thomson had the sense on his side, but then Hidlcs had the laugh, and in conse- quence was- the favourite in -the ward. 'My attention became completely taken up with my patient, Who, had sunk into a vary low state now that he was quietly in bed. I had done all I could for him' and was occuMed in another part of the Ward, when I saw Sister Janet bringing a woman up to his bedside. I was sorry to see he had such belongings, for he seemed to be a respect- able, decent young fellow. This woman was the most liisreputable object' you can imagine. Her battered bonnet kept slipping back off her head, in spite of her aimless clutches, and her ragged shawl was of a dirti- neis unspeakable. Anderson, my patient, was so ill that When Sister Jane Moved away I came forward to keep an eye on things. He sat propped up with pillows i on account of the njtiry to his jaw, and he could not reply to his mother's remark, except by feeble signs. But this did not seem to matter much. She was very voluble, and addressed herself to me and to Hicks in the neighbouring bed. She said all in a breath what - & pity it was when a fine young man like her son, and the only support of his widowed mother, took to drink, and how she begged and prayed of himYto leave it off, as sure she was that no good would come of it, and now her words hail come true, for he had fallen down the height of a flight of stairs on to the stones, along of the 'railings giving way when she was a-getting him up as drunk as anything, and naiv here he was, and she with- out a farthing, and would I kindly lend her a trifle; and she ended with a burst of tears. Of course, I could see what Sister Janet, being rather inexperienced and charity itself, had not noticed—that the woman was herself under the influence of drink and must be got away as quickly as possible, Which I proceeded to do. Of course, the scene was witnessed by all the patients near at hand. I I fancied Hicks looked somewhat abashed, though he was reading his paper with great diligence. I suppose he expected Thomson to improve the occasion for tee- totalism; but Thomson, with, I thought, some delicacy, left the incident to point its own moral. It must have been an hour after the departure of the •mother when Sister Janet beckoned me across the ward. • "Here is another person asking for No. 9," she said. "They should not have given another pass to-night. I can't let her in. She came just after the other woman was gone, and she has been standing outside for above an hour. Try and see if you can persuade her to go." I went out. What a contrast from No. 9's last visitor! A small, slim girl, pale as death, but quite collected. She clasped her hands. " Ah, if madame would permit me within!, It is his mother that was come. That-she has made harm, it is possible, yes. But I would not make him harm, me. I would regard only, and is it that madame thinks it would make him harm? Ah, non, impossible !" " Are you his wife ?" The pale face flushed. " Ah, non, to-morrow, madame we marry ourselves." ' Poor things! I felt for them. But I told her it was better for him to be kept quiet, and that she could some and sit with him to-morrow; being visiting afternoon. "But, madame, if he die! It is necessaire that I speak to him, all it is niScessaire." I told her that he was not dangerously hurt, that being a strong, sober, young man, there was every chance of a speedy recovery, and that as his jaw was hurt he could not speak to her if she went to him. "I will expect, madame, all the night, if it is ndces- sake, I will expect till he sleep, if I Tay then regard him." _ _
ANCE.
ing.

I could resist the pleading no longer, and I suspected Sister Janet of sending me to the task because she was unable to do se:. I went back to her. No, it would not do, she could not go back from her word. However, she finally gave way so far as to consent to the girl's coming inside and looking at Anderson from where he could not see her. Then she went away somewhat pacified. I offered to give any message she liked. " Ah, non, madame," she said, "you are so good. I thank you from my heart. But madame understands the wards must come from me to him. Tell him that I eome—that is all." The girl was very winning. As the hours passed, Andersen, distressing though his condition was, uttered no sound of complaint, and once when I 'adjusted his pillows and got a spoonful of milk between his lips with great effort, he managed to say, "I feel ever so much better." And the night nurse told me next morning that he had been just as patient during his sleepless night. The little French girl came that afternoon at the earliest moment of visitors time and stayed till the latest. She sat by the bedside and held his hand, as quite as a little mouse. She did not appear to say much, but I suppose they had a language of their own. She came every week. His mother also came, but not so regularly. The girl never yielded her place to the elder woman, but sat still by the bedside, looking at her all the time with an extraordinarily fierce expression. Tlie woman seemed to be cowed by it, and never stayed long. I was so interested in the two young people that I used to watch them as I sat at my needle- work at the end of the ward. I wondered what was going on below the surface. It was evident that the elder woman and the younger were not friendly to. each other. The young man, I thought, between the two; might have a difficult position. He went on fairly well for some time, and by degrees grew able to speak and eat with comfort, but his arm did not progress as it should. It was a very bad case of what the doctors call a compound comminuted fracture. How the accident happened remained a mystery. I had my suspicions, but could make nothing out clf Alderson, who was ex- tremely reserve& When I asked him how he came to tumble downstairs like a baby, he .nswered that he sup- posed it was along of clumsiness, and that in theiwalace the stairs .were dark and rotten. But I could not believe he had.fallen without a cause, and as 'I felt sure) the cause had not been drink. I could not help suspecting there had been some foul play. He had been in hospital a month or five weeks when' the doctors began to look very grave over the arm, and at last one morning they broke it to him that it would have to be amputated. I did not hear how he took it at' the first, for I went into the ward kitchen on. pretence of fetching something for the doctors, and cried. Such a' finer good young fellow, just going to be married, and by trade a carpenter 1 I said to myself that he would bear it like a man. But when I got back, to my surprise' found the doctor much out of patience. Anderson had flatly refused to have it taken off ! "Here, nurse," cried the aoctor," you come and talk to hina,and persuade the silly fellow not to throw away his life," and he left me to the task. We nurses are used to bringing a bright face and firm voice to such tasks as these, even when our hearts are sore, as mine was then. But it was of no use Anderson, poor, fellow, seemed as if turned to stone; all the life had gone out of his face, lie was hard and silent, and replied to me. only by curt refusals. This state of things went on for some days. Every morning the ; doctors tried again, but I left off arguing, for I saw it was of no use. However, I locked to visitors' day to change his mind, and only wished it had been nearer, for his arm was in a terrible state. And yet I dreaded it too, thinking of the shock the news would be to the poor little French sweetheart who had been hoping so soon to ,be his wife. Would she have nerve enough -to set aside her own feelings and try to reconcile him to the loss of his arm, and the altered life before him? The afternoon arrived, and I saw poor Anderson with a face that made my heart swell with pity watching the- door. But she was not as punctual as usual. Pie after- noon wore on, the visitors left the ward, and she had not come. The mother came and stayed a few moments only, looking scared, I thought. I did not hear any- thing that passed between them. She looked to me somewhat the worse for drink. I do not know phen I

aye been more taken in than by that girl's not appear mg. I had counted on it with such certainty. I could Ixscarcelpbelieve that the time was gone, even while I looked at the clock. As for the poor fellow, I could only guess what he felt. "Do you know why your friend has not come to see you to-day?" I asked him, as carelessly as "could. He was so shy of talking about himself that I was afraid of scaring him. He only said, "No, I don't; not for cer- tain;" but he looked at me as if he wanted to tell me more, and I thought it would come. And so it did that night when I gave his medicine. He said, just as I was leaving him, "I say, nurse, I want to send a letter." "Do you ?" I said; "I will write it for grou with pleasure. Who is it to be sent to ?" though, of course, I knew. "It's to my girl," and he grew red and very bashful. "I suppose you want to tell her about your arm?" " She-knows that. There was a man went out yester- day that lives in our yardiand he told my mother, and she told her." So this was the end of the little French girl's devotion! Now that there was no chance of his being able to keep her she would not even come to see him. As I could not say what I felt, I held my tongue. Anderson went on, "Will you say in the letter that she needn't be afraid of me wanting to keep her to her word? Tell her I ain't going to have my arm off. I'll take my chance. I don't want anything from her, but just to come once to see me for the sake of old times. Don't forget to put that in, nurse—for the sake of old times. Perhaps she is in the right of it to keep away; but I'd rather she'd come, ust for once do you see ?" I wrote the letter and posted it. I should like to have added a few words of my own to the young lady, but I thought I had better not meddle. Would you believe it? No answer came' from that heartless girl. The arm was getting Worse, and the doctors said that nothing but amputation could save his life. But Anderson couldn't be moved from his resolve. He said that if die he must, why he could die like a man, but that he'd known a fel- low that kept his leg for twenty years after the doctors wanted to cut it off. But he was so low and looked so )4opeless, that I fear he did not care much which way it went, and that was terribly against him. He needed something to give him heart enough to face life afresh as a cripple, and to bring himself to beg for such work as a cripple can do—he who had been a skilled artisan, an aristocrat of labour. A woman who loved him might do it, I thought; but visiting day came round, and again the mother came, but no sweetheart, and there could no longer be any doubt of her faithlessness. I begged Anderson to take it like a man, give up thinking of her, and have his arm off next morning. I told him that it was pride that stood in his way, but that he would show a far better kinci of pride in submitting to the will of God, and making the best of his misfortune like a brave man. He listened to me with attention, and though he did not answer, I saw I had made an impression ; though, I am sure as I spoke, find thought of his ruined life, I felt how different a thing practice and precept are., By and by he said, Nurse, perhaps I didn't ought to say it, but I can't trust to what my mother says. I can't get to the bottom of what she told me this afternoon. She's a spite against my girl on account of my taking to her. 11 You go out of doors, don't you nurse ?" He asked this so wistfully that I hastened to assure him I would go anywhere he liked for him in my off- duty time. So it was settled I should go to the house where his mother and the girl both lodged, and see if all was right. Happily, I had leave of absence that evening after tea. "You see my mother is overtaken with the drink now and again," he said, in a shame effaced under- tone, "and she has a terrible grudge against Marie, on account of its being along of her that she was put out with me; and you see Marie don't make, no allowance for her being in the drink that evening. And she don't know what fear is, that girl. She'll up and say anything - to the old woman." In his excitement he never saw that he was letting out his secret. I held my peace and marvelled at the absence of bitterness towards the mother who had been the cause of his misfortunes. I had no difficulty in finding the court to which Ander- son directed me. -It was such a place as none but the London poor are doomed to live in. I should not have relished going into after dark but for my nurse's garb, in which we are safe anywhere. And if I had been timid I need only have addressed myself to a policeman and he would have walked with me anywhere. So many of the force have been nursed by us that they are always pleased to show us attention. I had made up my mind to see the girl herself, if pos- sible; but when I made my inquiry for her of the grimy person who lived, with many others, no doubt, on the ground floor, I found that she had left the house! Did they know where she was gone? No, they did not, nor did they know whether Mrs. Anderson was in. I might go up and see, if I liked, upon which they disappeared into the gloom, and banged a door. I thought I had better try "going up," and it was well I did so, for I met a tidy-looking woman coming down, who not only could tell me that she had seen Mrs. Anderson go out, but that she knew where the young woman had gone to, but would not tell me unless I wanted it "far her good." So I got her address and went to find the place, though I half repented me of the errand, for this changing lodg- ing secretly, as if to cut off all appeal, seemed to me the most heartless thing the young woman had done. "Three pair back" being the direction I received at the front door, I groped my way upstairs as pitch dark as they usually are in such houses, and in answer to my tap Marie herself appeared at the door. The room was as neat as possible and quite pretty in its poor way, and she herself dressed in a trim dark dress with snowy French cap and apron. But it was only in the moment that passed before she recognised me that I had the heart to observe all this. Poor child, how she cried! I am afraid I began by being harsh to her, being so full of her supposed heartlessness. "Ah, madame, is it that he thinks me faithless? Madame, since I could not go to-day I write to him even now, voyez-vous." And I saw that she had been sitting with pen and paper before her. "Ah, he, pauvre garcon! I could not go, non; I am blanchisseuse:at!the French laundry and the principal change itself:;" and she know not me and permit me not to go at the right hour, and last week I go plus tard, and they say no, it is past the hour, and then I write a word and give it to the com- missionaire to give to my Jean. And is it that he had the heart to forget it? ma's old, it must be so. And is it possible that mon pauvre Jean think me faithless? Ah, madame," and the poor girl sobbed and cried so bitterly that I put my arm round her and made her lean on my shoulder. She was so absorbed in the piteous idea of Jean's suffering through doubts of her love that she seemed hardly to take in the idea,rof his losing his arm. "His mother say she tell me? Ah, non, she nevare tell me, madame; and the letter I have not receive it, non. I come away because that his mother is so mechante, so bad. She hate me for that Jean love me. Madame knows that she made to fall my Jean because we marry our- selves next day, and that he work for me then. Ah, he is too good to her; but then, voyez-vous, she is always his mother, yes." "She might forget her anger now that he is able to work for neither of you," said I. Marie ceased crying, and drew herself away from my arm, looking at me with a pale fixed face, as on the first occasion r had seen her.

" Ah, le-pauvre ange, his arm, I forget. Madame says he will lose it. Tell me." I told her all about it, and of his refusal to submit to, the operation. "Maas comment, my Jean is no coward !" and her eyes flashed. "He is desole that he cannot work, say you? But I can work—me! I work well. I get the good wages; and if I will not work! And as you say, madame, in your so kind way, one can do much with one arm, if one cannot be carpentare. Ah, how that God is good, for it, is the left arm, n'est-ce, pas, that he will lose 1" "Come back with me now," I said, "and persuade him to have it done to-morrow morning" (I did not like to say "before it is too late"). "I will get you in, and we must hurry, for my time is nearly up." "If I will come!" said Marie, and she was ready in a moment. I left her waiting down stairs while I went to Sister , Janet, who was only too glad to obtain admittance for ' her, and she was soon at the bedside of her "Jean." Of 6 course, I did not hear what passed betweete,them. When she went away Marie threw her arms round me and kissed me and smiled, with the tears running down her cheeks. The smile was one of pride and thankfulness, ' and the tears were for poor Jean's arm that was goin,f to be taken off next morning. Anderson's face when I went to him did me good to see, for- hope:, and life had come back into it. "I've changed my mind, nurse," said he, "and I know you'll be glad to hear it," and then he whispered, "I don't want any medicine, my gip has been enough medicine for me IP—E.. E. CHURCH PATRONAGE BILL.—The House 'having gone into committee on the Church Patronage Bill, the Marquis of SALISBURY proposed an amendment, with the object of carrying out the view he expressed in.tlie dis- cussion on the second reading, viz., that the 'Council of Presentation should begot rid of. It appeared to him that the Council was objectionable becaur,e it was introducing the principle of election into tbe management-of presenta- tationa, and also because it put men on trial as to , their character before men who were elected judgeerand thus introduced a principle which hitherto we had carefully kept at a distance. 'But the greatest objection of all was that the proposal would remove from the 'bishop a responsibility which was justly his, and which he could at any time better discharge than anyone else. The other function of the Council was to decide whether the sale of an advowson should •take place or not, and to accept advowsoiss from persons desirous of entrusting advoweons to them. The bill forbade the sale of advowsona by auction, and also the sale to clerical agents, and his impression was that when they had displaced these two branches of the traffic, the sale of advowsens would be a very rare occur- rence. He, therefore, considered it unnecessary to bring in this elaborately-elected Council for so small a purpose. The simplest way of dealing with the question was to purge the Council of Presentations out of the till, and, in pursuance of that object, be moved his first amendment, for the purpose of providing a Council which should determine whether in the case of an advoweonithe proposed purchaser was person who ought to hdld patronage or not. He pro- posed. that that Council should consist of the Bishop, the Archdeacon, the Chancellor .of the diocvrce, the Rural Deno, and two laymen, to 'be ,nominated by the Lord High Chancellor.—The Bishop of LONDON thought it of great importance to keep the Bishop out of contact altogether with the sale of livings, and sug- gested thatthe duties which the bill would impose upon him in thatrmatter should be discharged by the Chancel- lor of the diocese.—Lord GRIMPTHORPE recommended that in place of Lord Salisbury's proposal an amendment Should be inserted providing that no presentation should be valid without the approval in writing of a council, consisting of the Bishop of the diocese, the wicar-general, or chancellor, the archdeacon, and rural dean and one layman appointed by the bishop, who might make such inquiries astheymight think fit regard to the fitness of the person proposed to be presented;but should not decide against him without bearing him if ,he should require it. —The Bishop of LICHFIELD had placed on the paper amendments of the same scope and tendency as those of the noble Marquis, his desire being to nia.k.e a clean sweep

EXECUTION oF TffE OLIN-TAAL - POISONER. Early on Monday a heavy hailstorn passed over Liverpool, accompanied by a peal of thunder and a flash of lightning. This was followed by a fall of snow, which, however, had ceased shortly before the hour fixed for the exe- cution of Elizabeth Berry, at Walton Gael. The snow lay thickly on the gronnd, and the air. was bitingly kcen. Outside the gaol a very spaiM crowd had collected, consisting principally of rem on their way to work. Mrs. Berry was executed far the murder of her daughter, Edith Berry, by poises. ing her at Oldham, where she had .gone on a visit to her mother, who was a nurse in the infirmary there. On Sunday the condemned woman paid great attention to the ministrations of the t chaplain, and seemed quite resigned to her fate. 1 The scaffold was erected over a deep pit, specially made, in a shed in the prison yard. The convict was pinioned, and the procession to the scaffold. was immediately formed, headed by the chaplain. The convict came next, with her eyes closed, and. supported by two female warders. On turning the corner which brought her in view of the scaffold, she opened her eyes, and appeared to faint away. She was hurried forward the few remaining paces, and quickly placed under the beam. The chaplain read the usual service, to which the unhappy woman made the responses in an audible voice. The bolt was drawn, and the woman fell out a sight. The execution appearPd to be carried out im all respects well; and death seemed almost, if not quite, immediate. The doctors descended the weR by a ladder, and took the usual observations of the pulse. The chaplain was asked as to the words used by the culprit on the scaffold. He said they were: May God forgive Dr. Patterson r 'nig same remark she had made during the process a pinioning. The convict, being a small and light woman, was given a drop of 6ft. Gin. The chaplain states that the culprit was very attentive to hie ministrations, but she declared her innocence to the last. The execution was the first that has ever taken place at Walton Gaol. The Governor of the gaol states that Mrs. Berry made a tacit confession of her guilt, inasmuch as us a petition she drew up herself and sent to the Home Secretary, she stated that if she did poison her child she must have been insane at the time. On Sunday evening she made a statement to the chap-. lain, in which she asserted her innocence, and said that if her child had been poisoned it must have been by the creosote mixture prescribed by Dr. Patterson, the medical officer of the Oldham Work- house, who, it may be stated, was one of the princi-. pal witnesses against her at the trial. An inquest on the body of the executed woman was held on Monday within the prison by Mr. Aspinall, the Liverpool coroner. The jury viewed the body, which had been laid out in the dead- house of the prison, whither it had been conveyed after removal from the scaffold. The governor of the gaol gave evidence identifying the body, and. stating that the execution was most efficiently per- formed, death being instantaneous. The usual ver- dict was returned.

b Thp nu`" has been a gallant attempt to a, -, ~e 'ink `Mngs by means of the Round Table ';ll,t nrence, but it has not succeeded. From '4 tbeech which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN made ZSa-ttirneping of the National Radical Union L-rual' 'twould seem that if he cannot „is i ;leg 1., way there will in the future be some- "II l`ce War to the knife between Liberals tt Lib tlt eral Unionists. He does not, of tl., se, 1 . 00k at the issue in this light; but 1 Alt 1% What • t/ • -at WP shall see if the policy which' fl es - . ' e ,_"es IS ultimately carried out. He has the`u the conclusion from what took place! 4ilt herec,ent election at Burnley, and from it . had previously noted, that "party. ,tt:ls the strongest public sentiment in NlSce illtrl;trY with which we have to do ;" and impossible to get Liberal Union- b„-, uedy to vote for a Tory Unionist, it (it Inlrin:e duty of the Radical Union to pro- Otra-CA Cal Unionist candidates at the next ~ ,At Election in order, if need be, to pltl;l,slli:ibt,riangular duel." This is perfectly. Tile. 'e as a policy ; but, if carried out, it Per iltlic,4, fectly suicidal so far as the Liberal .1114!t Alest are concerned. This is so obvious ,Itt lyr ~..,armot but express our astonishment b-', • "-'IIAMBERLMN should hive run him- iv' tler(4ll such a queer corner. Take the case Ittl ev A Which the • self •'e right hon. gentleman 4,(1111c1 belt's, and let us try to realise what ba"iaye been the result if a triangular 11;*kgq ,i_ueen fought at the last election. Mr. 4teh otib.„`ire Liberal candidate, was returned Itt °llat tweek by a majority of shu t, ti ; th liere h ha e issue might have been different e 1 d also been a Liberal Unionist in (Illt (I, s -11 trid that nobody out of Bedlam will I, d the _ at the Liberal Unionist would have ;,!tlie ti!'neallest chance of being returned. It Lib " late Mr. R NDS was returned as hi, era' vtiot eitlei Unionist,,L but there was no trian- k the great majority of the tark qxt;Thtained were Tory votes. Alder- -166 vo, 4-wrnOD, who opposed him, polled tea as the Liberal candidate pure and 1

simple. Taking this as the full strength of the Liberals apart from the Unionists, how suggestive it is as to what would have hap- pened, at the last election, with a Liberal Unionist also in the field. The Tory can- didate, in such a contest, would have stood where he was with 4481 votes; Mr. SLAGG would at the least have polled as many votes as Mr. GREENWOOD obtained as against Mr. RyLANDS, namely, ,i66;+ and the Liberal Unionist would have been credited with 860 votes—which may be taken to be the outside number of the Liberal Unionists who swelled Mr. SLAGG'S majority. The result would have been that the Tory candi- date would have been returned with a ma jority of 315. while the Liberal Unionist would have been nowhere in the race. Burn- ley, it must be remembered, is a stronghold of Liberalism, and where parties are more evenly divided, as, for instance, at Warring- ton and St. Helens, it will be seen that it would be absolute madness to bring a Liberal Unionist in the field wits any hope, in a triangular duel, of his surviving as "the fittest." Mr. CHAMBERLAIN seems to think that if his plan were tried, it would enable the Liberal Unionists to know the "full strength of their party ;" if he had said sheer weakness we could have agreed with him. They might make some sort ofa show at the foot of the poll in each constituency, but so far as the House of Commons is concerned, they would be wiped out as a party. " The triangular duel" would, it is true, ensure a large majority of Unionists, but they would be Tory Unionists; and we have too much re- gard for Mr. CHAMBERLAIN as a Radical to suppose that, under any circumstances, he would deliberately set to work to bring a mis- fortune of that kind upon the country. Turning to another phase of the question, it is to be noted that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, un- able to come to an agreement with his colleagues of the Round Table, seeks to throw upon Mr. GLADSTONE, the sole respon- sibility of the failure of the 'Conference. " There is one man, and one man Only," he says, " who can restore unity to the Liberal party, and that is Mr. GLADSTONE;" and we gather from other observations that thc; mem- ber for West Birmingham desires it to be inferred that Mr. GLADSTONE is at present blocking the way. This is, as it seems to us, rather a cool way on the part of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN of getting out of the difficulty in which he finds himself. It comes to this that having made it clear to the leader of the Liberal party that he (Mr. CHAMBERLAIN) cannot give way one inch on certain points, that leader must be held to be responsible for whatever may happen if he does not immediately give way to his un- bending lieutenant. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN' seems to forget that there are certain things which even Mr. GLADSTONE cannot do; he cannot carry the Liberal party with him, now that Home Rule is the first plank in its plat- form, if he deviates by a hair's breadth on the question of principle. Not that there is any danger of him taking up a fresh position. T-he leader who has rallied his forces, under assaults from within and without, until they stand a solid compact body which is gaining energy and enthusiasm day by day. is not likely to change his ground at the bidding of half-hearted recruits who have lit le or no regard for the victory to be won. If Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is in favour of the principle of Home Rule, let him be content to see that, and that alone, inscribed pn the banner, and be willing to march forward in the full assurance that when the battle is won the victors will not abuse the golden opportunity which will be afforded them. He is at a turning point in his career; it is for himself and not Mr. GLADSTONE to determine whether he shall be known in history as the advocate or opponent of freedom for Ireland.

ANOTHER attempt has been made on the life of the EMPEROR OF RussrA ; but it has fortunately failed. There seems for some time back to have been reason to conclude that the conspirators of Russia were not idle. although little had been heard of them, for it has been noticeable that the greatest precau- tions were taken to protect the CZA.R in all his movements. The attempted assassination was made in the present instance while the EMPEROR was returning from a visit to the chuich connected with the Fortress of St. Peter and St. Paul. There are various versions of the incident. One account states that a bomb was thrown under the carriage, and it was to have been exploded by pulling a string attached to it ; but the would-be assassin, in the excitement of the moment, failed to hold the string ; and it thus luckily happened that the shell proved harmless. As evidence of the extraordinary ingenuity which had been exercised, it may be staled that the shell was in the form of a book, and was being carried as a book openly in the hand. A fellow conspirator, who was also arrested, was found with another shell in his possession, shaped like a leather pouch ; and, as might be expected, a considerable quantity of dynamite was discovered at the house where they had been lodging. It is believed that the conspiracy of which this diabolical outrage is the immediate outcome is exceedingly wide in its rAmifications, and already, it is reported, that 4, hundreds of arrests have been made." There seems to be some uncertainty at present as to whether the conspirators are Nihilists or Panslavists. If the latter, it is concluded that their object is to terrorise the EMPEROR into taking action in Bulgaria. These fanatics desire war to be declared rather than see Russia thwarted in carrying out what they believe to be her mis- sion ; and there is only too much reason to fear that the CZAR may be tempted to listen to counsels of this kind in the belief that war would divert attention from himself. A Vienna correspondent says the object of the plot which has been discovered was to over- turn the existing authority and establish a constitutional form of government. What- ever may be its origin, sufficient is known to justify the inference that it has its roots in the discontent gf the people Niiith a tyrannical autocracy. -Education is making headway in Russia as elsewhere, and thinking men are naturally impatient of being treated as if they , were children. They want a voice in the management of their own affairs, and when i the fathers are sent to Siberia, or put to death, for speaking out, we need not be sur- prised—much as we may r.gret it—that the sons respond with dynamite bombs. The situation is pitiful—almost hopeless. It is impossible not to sympathise with the Em- peror who is born to such.an.beritage of woe. He is compelled to fly like a criminal from his own capital. and shut hmself in a palace which is a dungeon to him, with the feeling that every man's hand is raised against him. Should he dream of granting a Parliament to his people, he is met with the fierce opposi- tion of the aristocracy, who fear that their privileges would be gone ; and there is be- sides the natural dread of giving play to forces
which might prove to be beyond control. Unhappy CXAR I He is a prisoner in his own palace. Hc wears the crown; but how gladly would he change it, if he could, for the peasant's cap

div.p: _ TIE .EXAMINER -ATURDAY, MARCH 19, 1887.
THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MARCH 19. 1887.
"TOUCH AND GO."

People are asking "Why should Tuesday. the 21St of June, be the National Holiday for the Jubilee celebrition, seeing that the Queen completes the so th year of her reign on the Monday ?" Our P.D. has a very good answer ;he votes for Tuesday, he says, be- cause he reckons himself" sure of Monday.'

The new Board of Directors of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company are reported to be hard at work in preparations for floating the scheme in such a way that it shall not fail. It is rumoured that a great deal of the money required has already been subscribed privately. This seems too good news to be true. Those who are " in the swim" speak, at any rate, with great confidence. It is understood that the Prince of Wales will cut the first sod.

" Sweet are the uses of adversity." Mrs. Jerome, the mother of Lady Randolph Churchill, was, it is stated, paralysed and bed-ridden at Cannes, when an earthquake shock caused her, in her fright, to take to her feet, and " she has been able to walit ever since," One has heard of pills against the earthquake ; but here is the earthquake itself as a remedy.

There are a great many people who are in favour of some amendment being made in the Limited Liability Acts. Company Mon- gers, as the law stands, have altogether too much of their own way. Was it " Biglow," or was it some other Yankee, who wrote ? Ido believe in Companies when they are safe, but some Are hollow, as the poet says, as hollow as a drum.

March, reversing the usual order of things, came in "like a lam." and will probably go out " like a lion." Meantime it is behaving like a tiger—the weather is absolutely fierce. How much better if we could only, as Shake- spere has it, look on —daffodils That come before the swallow dares and take The winds of March with beauty.

--- Executions are revolting, and especially when are culprit is a woman; but so long as the death punishment is carried out, it must be enforced against such fiendish creatures as the Oldham murderess. The cold-blooded villany of the murder of her own child was equalled only by her rank hypocrisy while under sentence. It is well for the world that we know of but one Lucretia Borgia and one Elizabeth Berry.

There is something wrong with the law which permits of brine pumpers under- mining, the Northwich man's property, and then denies him compensation because it cannot be said with certainty whose pump has done the damage. What if the property owner were knocked on the head by half-a- dozen brine pumpers? Would they be al- lowed to escapp because there had been so many "on the job ?" Or would it not be decided the whole gang should be punished?

Madame Bernhardt, fresh from South America, has just been interviewed in New York. Referring to the possibility of hostili- ties between France and Germany, she said : —"The talk of war made the young men in my company very excited. They all wanted to join the flag, but I asked them what I should do if they left me alone in South America, so they stayed." Of course they stayed. How could Sarah's young men leave her so far away from home—even if there was a prospect of bathing themselves in gore?

I Sir George Trevelyan says that of all the tempestuous causes in which he was ever engaged the reconciliation of the Liberal party is the best worth fighting for. Sir George is more than "a brick ; " he is a cart load of 'em. If Mr. Chamberlain would but rise to the height of this sentiment he would cease to talk about his Plan of Campaign. " Think'st thou it honourable, Coriolanus. for a noble man still to remember wrongs?" That, too, is a sentiment which might be commen- ded to his attention.

Mr. John Dillon, M.P., commands the respect even of his enemies by his transparent sincerity; but he is just now allowing his zeal to run away with his discretion. Refer- ring to reductions in rents, at a mass meeting in Tipperary, he said :—" I think it would be only fair-play that, supposing we asked 25 per cent, without a Coercion Act, we should ask 4.5 per cent, if we got a Coercian Act." To fight in this way is, however, to strike at random. Why should a landlord, Irish or English, suffer for the sin of the Govern- ment ? Fair-play by all means; but let it be fair-play.

"Bill Stickers" is a grasping fellow; he will have it. One of his kin claimed £3lO from Mr. J. W. Sidebottom, M.P., for helping him to win the Hyde Division of Cheshire by plastering walls, dzc. He thought this was coming it "a teettle too strong ;" and a refer- ence has resulted in the total being reduced to 192 149. Now, if printers could only get paid after this fashion those who hold shares in certain companies would be happy: dividends would always be forthcoming. But your Master Printer is looked upon as " small beer" compared with "Bill Stickers."

Apopos of the elevation, on Monday, of five prelates to the Cardinalate, it is interest- ing to come across the following editorial gag, which appears in the story of "Seth's Brother's Wife," in the current issue of " Scribner's Magazine." Tom Watts is giv- ing his views as to " How it's done," and he says: " It is just as well to sling in some items of your own, such as There is a grow- ing abuse among the Baptists to have Bishops like other people,' or It is understood at the coming Consistory the Pope will create seven new American Cardinals.' That last item is a particularly good • point. Every once in ' a while predict more Cardinals. It doesn't hurt anybody, and it makes you look solid when anything does happen." •

Some people will be horrified with the knowledge that there has been an inter- change of presents between the Pope and the Queen. They will conclude that :England is rushing headlong to destruction, or into the arms of the Pope, which, to them, is the 'same thing. But why shouldn't the head of the Catholic Church and the Sovereign of England be amiable with each otht r ? It is better than hurling anathemas—or bomb- shells.
TRIPLIS BIRTH AT WIDNES.—The wife of MT. William Jones, labourer, of Gossage -street, gave birth to three girls a few days ago, all of whom, however, have since died. The mother is doing, well,
