Sr. JOHN'S A MBIII.A.NCE ASSOCIATION, WIDNES —D r. MacLennan on Wednesday evening examined 30 members of the Whines branch on Wednesday evening, and the re• UltS were highly satisfactory. The successful membsrs will each receive a certificate.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.—Up to last night only the five retiring members, Messrs F 11 Goseige, E Carey, T Handley, H Gaskell, jun., and S Sadler have been nominated. They are the nominees of the Owners and Occu- piers' Association. A widespread feeling prevails that the representatives could not at present be much improved, but 1 there are rumours that several independent candidates will enter the lists, the name of the Rev G Bond, vicar of Farn• worth, being prominentlY brought forwafd, Wednesday nest is the lee day on which nominations can be received. HUTCHINSON-STREET PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OF HOPE, WIDNES.—In connection with this society, an enter- tainment was given on Tuesday evening by the members of the Simin's Cross Primitive Methodist Band of Elope, in Hutchinson-street Chapel. The various recitations, dia- logues, and vocal and instrumental selections, were gone through in a very creditable manner and were much appre- ciated. Mr. T. Marshall, who is conducting evangelistic services in Hutchinson-street Chapel, during the even- ing delivered an interesting address. Mr. S. Owens occu- pied the chair. HYDROPHOBIA IN RUNCORN POLICE DIVISION. —AS stated in this joarnal last Saturday, a dog which was suf- fering from hydrophobia had been destroyed on the estate of Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., Norton. In consequence of this circumstance Sunerintendent Hollingsworth on Mon- day asked the Runcorn magistrates for an order to be is- sued under the third section of the Dogs Act, 1871, in the Runcorn Division. compelling owners to confide their dogs until the first of May. He remarked that thi2 was the wish of the Chief Constable. Toe Bench granted the order, a copy of which may be Perused in our advertising columns.

POPULAR CONCERT AT RUNCORN—Another Of the popu- lar conceris arranged by the Mill Brow Military Band took place on Tuesday evening in Bet kesda Lecture Hall. Miss Edith Puckey, contralto, of the Liverpool Operatic Society sang several songs with cultured expression and taste, and she was henoured with an enthusiastic recall. A tenor w;th a voice of light pure tone, Mr Alex Coope was fairly suc• cessful, and Mr W Wilson caused much merriment by his humourous songs. Mr A E Pierpoint cleverly performed a gavotte from Mignon. As usual the band, under the able leadership of Mr T Outhwaite, played an admirable selec- tion of music to the enjoyment of those present. Mrs Kay and Mr W Dennstt acted as accompanists.

BENEFIT CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—A concert arranged for the benefit of a widow (Mrs. Beesley) and family at present in distressed circumstances was held in Runcorn Public Hall on Monday evening. Although a capital pro- gramme had been arranged, the audience was of the most meagre proportions, and the venture would result in finan- cial loss. Selections from the Messiah, by a well balanced choir of 60 voices, formed tbe first part of the entertain- ment, Mies Hammon, Miss Howard, and Messrs R Moore, A Fox, and C Pownall taking solos. After an interval songs were given by Miss Horton, Miss 4-lampoon (who secured an encore), and Miss Howard, and Mr R Morris and the gentlemen previously mentioned. The choir also sang several part songs in good style. Mr W Handley was the conductor, and Mr J Ravenscroft the accompanist. RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY COMMIWEE.—Tbe monthly meeting of this committee was held on Wednesday, at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road, under the presidency of Mr F A Lake, There were also present Messrs W Handley, T Riley, F J Norman, and J D Jones (librarian). The librarian reported that during February 1,998 banks had been issued to borrowers, showing an increase of 334 over the corresponding month last year. This was the highest total ever reached. Books presented during the month : By Mr John Simpson, Dr Rigg's "Comparative View of Church Organizations : Primitive and Protestant"; "A tour through Canada," and "The Wesley Naturalist" (monthly magazine); by Mr C Chivere, of Bath, "Pitman's Phonetic Dic,ionary."—Accounts were passed to the amount of £5l 7s 41, including £l5 10s for new books and £23 for rent.

SERIOUS OUTBREAK Or CATTLE DISEASE NEAR RUNCORN. —At Parkside Farm, Aston, occupied by Messrs Percival Bros., a serious outbreak of disease was discovered on Satur- day. Seven pies were dead, and other 19 of the herd of 128 animals were seriously ill. On Monday 32 pigs and three sheep were dead, and great fears were entertained that the disease would spread. Two veterinary surgeons. who were called in, described the disease as anthrax, and Superinten- dent, liellingworth, of Runcorn, at once issued instructions that no cattle, unless previously certified to be free from disease by a veterinary surgeon, were to be removed. By Wednesday the disease appeared to have been arrested, as no more deaths had occurred, but the present loss to Metiers Percival is very heavy. The seriousness of the outbreak will be understood when it is stated that Messrs Percival own upwards of 300 head of stock. .

THEATRE ROYAL, RUNCORN —poring the past week this place of entertainment has been nightly crowded with de- lighted audiences assembled to witness the sensational drama "Alone in London," performed by the company of Messrs. VVyrn Miller and T. F. Ellistow. The piece, which is replete with realistic situations, admirably depicted with scenic and mechanical effect, is in the hands of a strong combination, and each part received Its adequate represen• tation. Miss May Holt and Miss Lille Wylde in their re- spective characters of" Tom Chickweed" and Nan," have won unstinted commendation and as the villanous adven- turer Richard Radcliffe, Mr. Ernest Montefoire was a great success. Mr. W. P. Dempsey " Charlie Johnson," Miss Madge Douglas "Liz Jenkinson." Mr. Charles Hnntley sprigalee," Miss Clara Reed " Mrs Maloney," Mr. Walter Barton "Mr. Burnaby," Mr. L. Meadows" Jenkinson," and Mr. Magill' Martyn "John Biddlecomb," are each deserv- ing of praise for their able assumptions of the characters allotted to them.

A FATAL IMMEIRSION AT RIINCORN.—Air 3 E Worslev, the deputy coroner, on Tuesday afternoon, held an inquest at Runcorn on the body of James Rains, of 94, Church. street. On Friday afternoon the deceased and a man named John Gandy walked to Norton for Pleasure. As they were returning along the canal side permission was given them to go on board a passing boar. Mr Gandy easily succeeded in getting on hoard, but Mr Raine, who was 69 years of age, and a cripple, slipped in making the attempt, and fell into the water. He was quickly' rescued, and with the object of conveying him quickly home he was taken to a farm at Astmoor, where a carriage was engaged. Three hours, how- ever, elapsed before he arrived home, and he was then suf- fering so severely from the effects of the immersion that Dr Robinson was called in. He rapidly grew worse, and death ensued on Saturday night. A verdict that death was the result of natural causes, aggravated by immersion. Was re- turned. The deceased, who was a man ef Independent means, was one of the founders of the Primitive Methodist Sunday School in Runcorn, and he was much respected. ST. PATRICKs Day AT WIDNES.—The anniversary of the patron saint of Ireland was honoured by the Irish in- habitants of Widmes, in the quaint fashion that has charac- terised the event for many years past. The children at- tending the Catholic Schools, were granted a holiday, and were to be seen parading about the streets plentifully be- decked with green, which their elders also displayed., whilst those who could obtain it were adorned with a sprig of the shamrock. In the morning a well-attended service was held at St. Mary's Chapel, and in the afternoon about 200 members of the Young Men's Society, headed by their band, walked in procession through the Principal thorough- fares. In the evening the band of the Irish National For- esters also paraded the streets. A concert WAS held in the Volunteer Hall, in aid of the Irish Eviction Fund,•and the fund which is being raised for the purnose of building a new Catholio Church in the town. The building was crowded in every part, and both objects will receive sub- stantial help. The artistes were Cat Rooney (character comedian and dancer), Miss Constantino (ballad aid de- scriptive vocalist), Frank O'Grady and Helen Daley (come- dians and dancers), Mrs Horan, Mrs Welsh (known as the sisters Smaham), Messrs. F. G. Sydney (comedian), Kiddie (basso), and C. Finn (tenor.) Miss Cullen ably performed the duties of accompanist. The National and League of the Cross bands played selections. GYMNASTIC COMPETITION AT RIINCDRII.—At Runcorn Gymnasium on Saturday night the local team were pitted against New Brighton Gymnasium team in the second round of the competition for the Liverpool District Chal- lenge Shield. There was a fair number of spectators pre- sent. The visitors were led by Mr T. H. Wardleworth, and the local eight were conducted by Mr. E. Knowles, of Liverp3ol Gymnasium, wile is a native of Runcorn. Mr. W. Milner, of Liverpool Gymnasium, etiolated as judge, and he declared Runcorn the winners, by a rmajerity of 15 points. div.p: RUNCORN AND TIIE QCEEN'S JUBILEE.—The Board of Commissioners have suggested that the chairman (Mr. P. Speakman) shall call a meeting of ratepayers for the pur- pose of considering how the Jubilee of the Queen shall be clebrated. Mr. Speakman has fixed Thutsday evening I nest for the meeting. EVANGELISTIC SERVICES AT WIDNISS.—During the past week special evangelistic services have been conducted by Mr T Marshall, of Southport, in the Hutchinson-street Primitive Methodist Chapel. Mr Marshall also occupied the pulpit three times on Sunday. the seivices have been fairly well attended._

MAGIC LANTERN ENTERTAINMENT AT RUNCORN.—Before a large and delighted audience at Rt. Luke's School-roem, on Thursday night, Mr. W. Rhodes, by trl.:018 of a magic lantern exhibited a number of views illurtrative of the ex- pedition of the Alert and the Discovery to the Arctic regions Mr. J. J. Speakman presided. WIDNES C E.T.S.—The weekly meeting wee held in the National Scher)ls, on Thursday evening, under the presi- dency of the Vicar. The procerdings consisted of a concert of snored music, which was admirably rendered by the fol- lowing local vocalists :—Miss Broad, the Rev. J. R. Jones, , Mtssrs. L. and .J. Kilcross. W. White, and F. Scott.

FORTHCOMING BAZAAR AT RUNCORN.—On Wednesday and Thursaay next a baziar will he held in Regent-street school-room, Runcorn, with the object of reducing the debt on the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Greenway-road.—Dr. McDougall will perfolm the opening ceremony. Full par- ticulars may be re.id in our announcement columns.

Mr. W. H. JUDE'S MUSICAL EVENING AT RUNCORN.— Under the auspices of the Runcorn Y.M. C.A., Mr. W. H. Jude, principal of the Liverpool Organ School, will lecture On "The power of music," in Runcorn Public Hall, on Monday night. The eubjse will be illustrated with selec- done of music, and the public should not miss the omelet- [unity of having such a treat. WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB.—Although defeated in their contest against Warrington, the Widnes footballers have been feted this week. Mrs. Gerard,of the Alexandra Hotel, had promised the team a supper, on condition that they won the West Lancashire Cap, but her sympathy with them in their defeat induced her to entertain thean to a substan- tial meal on Inesday night. About 50 persons were pre- sent. Mr. Herriman, of the Mersey Hotel, also provided a capital repast for the teem and friends on Thursday even- ing, and afterwards the room was cleared for dancing. HOLY TRINITY Des SCHOOLS. RUNCORN. Last night the annual concert and distribution of priz,4t in Connection ! with these successful schools, took place in the Public Hall. An interesting muejcal programme was gone through by the children in capital style, the head master, Mr. T. H. Annetr, conducting the proceedings. A music,' sketch entitled "Old friends with new faces," by 10 scholars, was received with much favour by the large audience of parents and friends who had assembled. During an interval in the pro- gramme Mr. Clarke Aspinall, J.P., of Liverpool, delivered an eddrese, and subsequently he distributed the prizes and certificatee to the successful sclinlars. FOOTPATH OBSTRUCTION AT ‘RUNCORN.—On Monday, at Runcorn Petty &sabots, William Henry Dean, Joseph Cliff, Frederick Lamb, .fames Foster, and John Present, youths, were charged with obstructing the footpath in Halton-road. on the night of Sunday, the 6,11 in'.—fhe defendant pleaded guilty.—Superintsndent Hollingworth said the practice was becoming an intolerable nuisance not only OR a Sunday night, but on every other night. Youths of the description of the defendents smoked, spit, and insulted the people .who passed aiming. The Bench had previously threatened to -deal severely with these offenders, and he pressed tbie case.—Each defendant was ordered to pay lae incleding cos's.

FELONIES AT WIDNES —At Widnes Petty Sessions, OD Thursday, George Gervas, 14 years of age, was charged with stealing a weighing bean, worth is, the property of Sylvester Heaton, clogger, of James-street, Miws Bank.— The prisoner was ciught in the act of committing the rob- bery, and in answer to P C. Bruce, he said he took the 'seam because he thought it was of no uae.—He was fined 15s or a fortnight. —Thomas Longshaw, libaurer. Warrington, was charged with stealing two spades and a coat, the property of his employer, Edward Percy. contractor, Widnes. Toe prisoner was also charged with stealing a bottle of whiskey from the Millfield Inn, occorged by Thomas Lea. He was remanded until .Monday.

A Yost:NG THIEF AT Runcorett.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. J. Brundrit. Joseph Annabel, 15 years of age, was charged with committing s-tveral rob- heries. On Monday night, the manager of Egerton's sh-to in Bridge-street, miss•d a shirt, and acting under the advice of the police. he concealed himself to watch. In a few minutes the prisoner entered the shop, and after giving a glance round, picked up a pocket handkerchief. He was at once apprehended. In his possession were found several ties, a couple of linen fronts, a cardigan jacket (stolen from Messrs Egertons' on the 9th inst.), and a number of stolen articles were found at the house whore he lived in Itzutton- street.—The prisoner Was remanded until Monday. BRUNSWICK IMPROVEMENT CLASS. RUNCORN.—On Wed- nesday evening the lecture-room of the above society in Brunswick-street was occupied by members anxious to listen to an address by the Rev. A. P. Watson on " Some of the objects of mutual improvement classes." The reverend lecturer stated that as the result of a close scrutiny of varions programmes of such classes he had concluded the principal aims of the associations were to teach the mem- bers properly to read, to write, to think, and to speak, and in practical product to work, wisely and well, in the world and in the church. While giving, from personal exoerience, nsany useful hints to those wishing to attain these ends, as to manner and method, Mr. Watson introduced humourous anecdotes and succeeded in maintaining the interest of members. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the lec- turer for his services.! -

A WIDITF9 RTJFFIAN DFT9ERrEDLY PTINISNED.—Refore Messrs. G. Pilkington and T. S. Timrnis, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, William Welding, a middle•aged man, of Travis-street, was charged with having created a breach 0r the peace in Lugsriale-road by assaulting William Jones, lodging-house keeper. He was also charged with assaulting P.C. Chambers—On Saturday night the prisoner annoyed Jones by parading in front of his house, and making dis- cordant cries, and by insulting his daughter. Jones Corn- plainer] to Constable McGinis, who advised him to summon the prisoner. The prisoner was ordered away, hut instead of obeying him he struck Jones several times in a savage man- ner. He was at once appreheoded, and on the way to the police station he struck Chambers on the face, and kicked I him on the leg in a very violent manner—For the asstult on the officer the prisoner was sentenced to two month's bard labour, and for the assault on Jones he was ordered to find sureties for his good behaviour for six months, or to go to gaol for a month. • LEFF OUT IN THIS Coinr A RUNCORN LICHNSING CASN.—Before Mr, A. Thomas and Mr. G. L. Davies, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Francis Barker, land- lord of the Ferry Hotel, Church-street, was charged with having, on the 9th inst., kept open his premises for the sale of beer during prohibited hours, and also with permitting drunkenness to take place. William Hitchmough. of Church- street, was charged with being on the premises during pro- hibited hours, and further, with being drunk. Mr. A. Fletcher. of Northwich, defended. P.C. Millington deposed! that at 25 minutes past eleven, on the night of the 9th, the Ferry Hotel was open and he entored. In the kitchen he found the defendants. Hitchmough WaS drunk, and staggered out of the house when the officer entered. Jacob Hedley, butcher, proved that the house was open. For the defence Mr. Fletcher said the defendant Barker had lived in the house for 17 years, without the least Cause of complaint. and when their worships had heard the explanation he was suee they would be of opinion there had been no offence committed against the licensing law. When Mr. Hitch- mough returned home at half-past ten that night—he being , a man 72 years of age, who had had the misfortune to he three times married—(latighter)—he found that ' the lady who now called herself Mrs Hitchmough had retired. from the domestic scene, and had taken with her the whole of the household furniture, leaving him simply a bed, but no clothing to cover him. Mr. Barker, as well as being Mr. Hitchmough's tenant, was also his agent, and collected his rents besides doing other business of private character. It was natural that be should go to the man who had his con- Hence to tell his troubles, and accordingly he went to M. Barker's house to make arrangements for lodgiuga. In fact he slept at the Ferry Hotel that night and was living there still. He was not a customer in the ordinary sense of the , word. As to the charge of drunkenness this was denied. It was natural that the old gentleman should be very much put about with the state of things at home, and he was very much excited. He had not taken anything which would have made him intoxicated that night. The evidence of Mr. Barker having been given, the Bench dismissA the case.

SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A RIIICCORN At Runcorn Petty &salons on Monday, before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. G. L. Davies, W. J. Shore, shipowner, who is now going through the bankruptcy COttlt, charged with having on the 17th FO.ruarv, trivollod on L. dz N.-W. Railway between Runcorn and Rdge.E.Lil, without having previously paid his fare, with inter! to de- fraud payment. —The defendant plewied guilty. Mr. rand who represented the Company, said he consitlereeh it an aggravation of the offence if the person who .com trui ted it occupied a respectable position. 041 the day in question defendant was at Runcorn Station Irt ample time for the 10-2 S am, train for Liverpool, and he could have got a ticket had he chosen to do so. ;The ticket collecto-, who had had instructions previously au rut the defendant ant others, entered the train with the defendant. At Edge. Hill he sew the dtfendant leave the train and walk into the urinal, where he stayed for five or ten minutes. He then came on the platform and read a newspaper, and when the . train was coming in for Lime-street he w tu the book- ing-office and took a ticket for that station. A collector ' then demanded the defendant's ticket from Roner(l. replied that he had not come by troin, but ‘vhen the Run- corn collector appeared on the scone, he admitted his offence.—The defendant said ia derence that he could oulY sear that he win quite beside himself owing to distressing events. He had gone down to Edge Hill to meet 'a man from whom he had to receive some funds to pay an execu- tion or to call a meeting of creditors owing to recent rever- ses. He asked the Bench to be lenient because he had no funds, all his estate being in the hands of his trustee.—Mr. Brundrit said it was sad to' see- a man in the defendant's position brought up on a charge like this It was not-as if the offence had been committed inadvertently, because when challenged he denied having come by train, and there was no doubt it was a systematic fraud on his part, which ought to beipunished. It must have caused his wife and family great pain, but with that the Bench had nothing to do. A tine of 20s and costs, Z 1 3s Bd was imposed, or in default 14 days' hard labour. The defendant was allowed week is which to pay the money.

CHURCH OF HNGLAND TEMPERANCR SOCIETY, HALTON. —A meeting was held in connection with this society on Tuesday night in the girls' schoolroom, when the vicar, on behalf of the members of the committee, presented Miss Short with a school cabinet as an acknowledgment of her services to the society. The present was suitably inscribed, and was appropriately acknowledged by Miss Short. LECTURE AT WIDNES.—The Rev. It. G. Hughes, emigre- gatiooal minister, on Thursday evening delivered a lecture on The late Stephen Tanymarian, the great Welsh poet, musician, and preacher," in Milton Congregational Chapel, Simm's Cross.. Mr. Hughes treated his subject in an able and interesting manner, and it was rende.ed additionally entertaining by the vocal contributions of Miss Annie Wil- Berne, of Liverpool. Mr. J,hn Brock, J.P., presided. ST. PATRICK'S DAY AT APPLETON.—The festival of St. Patrick, the Patron Saint of Ireland, was celebrated on Thursday even:ng at Appleton by a varied entertainment of vocal and instrumental muck, and readings, given by mem- bers of the congregation, under ihe presidency of the Very Rev. Dean Finegan. The chairman delivered a brief pane gvric on the life of St. Patrick, his lab mrs, toils. so Hering, and ultimate success in tbe cause of Christianity. While 1 rejoicing at the devotion and unabated enthusiasm with which the Irish petiole always celebrate the enniversary of St. Patrick', he very muce regretted that Englishmen do not pay more honour to the Na,ional Patron Saint of this country. The artistes consisted of the Misses Leatherbarrow, Miss Moran, and Messrs Morrison, Finn, Hayes, and Dr. McCambridge as vocalists, and Miss Johnson and Mr. Cald- well as pianoforte accompanists. A notable feature ef this entertainment, and one which greatly coutributed to its success, was the introduction of clerical talent, by two read- ings given by Father Kavanagh, entitled, " Paddy the I piper," and "The gridiron," which elicited general ap- ' plause. The various performers acgoitt4ll themselves with commendable skill, arid, judging from the repeated encores and enthusiastic demonstrations of applause, the audience must /-ave been satisfactorily entertained. VACCINATION CIRCULA.R. The Local Govern- ment Board have issued a circular letter to all pub- lic vaccinators containing instructions for increased care to be taken in the vaccination of children, and also for extra precautions to be taken in regard to the lymph which is empbyed. A PARK FOR CREWE.—At a meeting of the foro- prietors of the London and North-Western Railway on Wednesday, some opposition was offered to the proposal to give a public park to Cr-ewe, but it was almost unanimoinly over-ruled. The'company Will give 30 acres of land and expend £lO,OOO in laying it out as a park.

Tan SPEAKER'S LEVEE.—The following gentle- men connected with this district were present at the Speaker's Levee on Wednesday evening:—Sir W. C. Brooks, Captain E. T. D. Cotton, Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, Mr. 11. J. Tollemache. Viscount Cross, Colonel H. B. 11. Blundell, Mr. A. H. Smith- Barry, and Mr. H. Seton-Karr. INCREASED SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION AT PEN- KETH.—PIans and specifications for the enlarge- ment of the Penketh Elementary School have been prepared by Mr. William Owen, of Warring- ton, and the work has been prepared by Mr. Joseph Lloyd, builder. The enlargement has been needed for some time, and the friends of the scheme have been zealously working in many ways to realise the required funds. It is intended to hold a bazaar in. Waiirington in aid of the object. .Trin DEATH OF Mn.. RANDLE WILBRAHAIL—The " Wprld" says :—Lord Lathom is placed in mourn- ing by the death last Thursday of his cousin, Mr. Randle Wilbraham, of lode Hall, Cheshire, a few days after attaining his eighty-sixth birthday. Mr. Wilbraham was a staunch Tory of the old " blue " type, and he was very popular in the county; while the fact that he was a practical agriculturist did not diminish the esteem in which he was held by his tenants. He is succeeded in the estates by his brother, General Sir Richard Wilbraham, K.C.B. THE ROBBERY AT BOLD.—John Beddard, a young man, residing at 8, Manley-street, Warrington, was brought up on remand at the Town Hall, St. Helens, on Monday, on a charge of stealing three brass candlesticks, valued at is 6d, from the Clock Face Inn, Bold, the property of Mary Bromilow. The prisoner had been with a party of footballers to St. Helens and when returning called at prosecutor's house. After they had gone the candlesticks were missed, and they were afterwards found in the pri- soner's possession. Prisoner had had some drink at the time and said he did not know how the can- dlesticks got in his possession.. A fine of .£2, or one month's imprisonment, in default of payment, was Imposed. THE HOME InoN TRADE.—There is as yet no greater animation in the English iron trade; but a, better feeling appears to be prevailing the market. Pig-iron has been far from active this week, and there is a further slight retrogression in prices. The Glasgow warrant market has been quiet. Little business has been doing. as the public still hold aloof, and the lower price is not tempting them to buy. The output of iron is still restricted, but it is felt that no impression is being made upon the al- ready excessive stocks. Closing buyers of warrants were on Wednesday 43s 2d cash, and 43s 4k4 a 1 month, sellers asking id per ton more. Saotch makers' iron is quiet, but priced are steadily main- tained.—lron.

A VETERAN TEMPERANCE WORKER. A pam- phlet, which will be of special interest to workers in the temperance cause, has just been published by Mr. John Heywood, with the title of "The Ups and Downs of William Gregson, for 50 years a Temper- ance Advocate." It is from the pen of Mr. S. M. Holden,who has done his work very satisfactorily. Dr. Lees contributes a framed preface; then there is a good portrait of Mr. Gregson; and a reprint of the poet Prince's poem" The angel of temperance." As Mr. Gregson ia known everywhere and every- where admired, there is reason to conclude that there will be a•large demand for this lively sketch of his lively, career. Mr. Gregson, who is still alive, is enjoying a well-earned repose at the age of 67' years. MANCH-287ER AND TM{ MERSEY DO= BOARD.— The withdrawal of the Dock Board (Various Powers) Bill from the group in which it was originally set down is in view of a hoped-for settlement on the point in dispute .between Manchester and Liver- pool. The negotiations which are slowly proceed- ing relative to an enlargement of the constituency ot the Board are being continued, and both are dis- posed towards an amicable arrangement.—From later information we learn that the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board has given notice of its intention to withdraw its various powers bill. The with- drawal of this bill has been brought about solely through the great opposition shown towards it, in , face of which it, was most unlikely that it would have been sanctidned by Parliament. LORD HARTINGTON ON TECHNICAL EDUCATION.— On Wednesday, in his address to the students of the Polytechnic Young Men's Christian Institute, Lon- don the Marquis of Hartington said it behoved Ettllishmen who desired to maintain their commer- cial supremacy to inquire how the nation was equip- ped for the keen competition with other countries. It was not yet too late for us to keep the position which up to the present we had i held n the incite- try of the world, but that could only be done by providing greater and, more improved technical education. The only question was how that should be provided. Employers of labour and trade unions seemed hardly alive to the urgency of the case Technical colleges had been established which gave the necessary instruction to the future managers and directors of our industries, but what was still deficient was the adequate technical and trade in- struction bf the labourers themselves. It was not to be expected that the State or voluntary effort should, provide all that was needed, and his lordship hoped that ere long municipal and local governing bodies would establish in every centre industrial and technical schools suitable to local needs and supported out of local funds. THR JUBILEE Exam-rim—The usual weekly meeting of the Executive Council was held on Mon- day, at the City Offices, North-Western Bank Build- ings, Dale-street, Sir David Radcliffe presiding. -There were also present the following members Messrs. William Bennett, H. Cookson, James Et- , helby, Meadows Frost, I. H. X Gill, John Houlding, ' F. J. Leslie, Richard Ripley', and W. J., Winstan/ey. The minutes of the various committees were con- ' sidered, and very interesting reports were received from the Commissioners of the War Trophies. and Indian and Colonial Courts. Promises have been received of rare and valuable specimens of arms and warlike appliances from Greenwich, NetleYt B ir- mingham, and the Tower" also of industrial aid 4 pictorial illustrations of our Indian and Colonial possessions from the South Kensington and other collections. The War Trophies Coramittee are engaged in securing works of art illustrative of the campaigns and naval engageme,ins during the pre- sent reign, which cannot fail to prove highly attrac- tive. The Old LanCashire Village is to be construc- bv ted on designs approved the Arts Committee, and prepared by one a the members; over one hundred shops will be put up to public competition in this interesting and picturesque portion of the Exhibition, preference being given to Liverpool , tradesmen, provided the exhibits intended to be , shown prove to be of a satisfactory nature to the , committee. A letter was read from Mr. Ellis Lever, of Manchester, expressing his gratification at the adoption of the scheme of exhibiting life-saving appliances both on sea and land, and intimating his readiness to give every assistance in his power in A furtherance of this object,

Holm Ruts Purzzix.—We have had forwarded to us one of these mechanical contrivances as ad- vertised in another column. To look at, it is the simplest of simplest things; but when the solution is attempted, it will be found- like Home Rule it- self—to test the wits of the wisest. The conditions under which Messrs. W. Winnett and Company offer prizes are very tempting, and should lead to a. rapid sale of the wonderful puzzle. Mn. GLADSTONE ON HOME RULE.-0/1 Thursday evening Mr. Gladstone addressed the Yorkshire Liberal members at the town house of Mr. Barran, M.P., and made an important speech on the Itish question. He declared that the demand of Ireland for local government was reasonable—by which was meant an effective self-government in affairs pro- perly and exclusively Irish, subject to the unques- tionable supremacy of the Imperial Phrliament He should always be ready to consider any proposal that the Liberal Unionists might make, but he claimed that the majority of the party must con- trol the policy of the party. With regard to the land question, he thought that a system of purchase • could be brought forward that would not pledge British credit.

THE PRINCE OF WALES, THE MA.NCHESTER Ex- , ararnow, AND THE SHIP CANAL.—The following letter has been received by the executive committee of the Manchester Exhibition :—" Marlborough House, 16th March, 1887.—My dear Sir,—The Prince of Wales has much pleasure in making arrange- ments which will enable him to remain two days at Tatton. He approves, therefore, of your sugges- tions that on the first day he should go and return by train to Manchester; that on alighting he should proceed to the Town Hall, thence to the Exhibition, where there would be provided luncheon; that he should open the Exhibition, and then return to Tat- ton, driving on his way to the station through a few streets. On the second day he would drive to Manchester, turn the first sod of the Ship Canal (if it is to be), lunch with the Mayor, and go to Lon- don by the 245 train. lam writing the purport of this letter to the Mayor.—Believe me, &c., Fruaims KNOLLYS."

WIDNES F.RBE PUBLIC LIBRARY.—To-day (Sat- urday) the reading room of the Widnes Free Public Library will be opened for the first time. Fifteen months has elapsed since the Act was adopted by the ratepayers, and during that period a building has been erected behind the Public Offices at a cost of .£l,OOO. Ample provision has been made for the lending library, and for the accommodation of readers. Owing to the labour involved in arrang- ing the books (which at the commencement will number upwards of 2,000), and in compiling a catalogue, the lending library will not be open for several weeks, but the reading room will be opened to-day. It is a commodious, well lighted, admir- ably ventilated, and comfortably furnished room, and will be supplied with the leading London and provincial daily and the local weekly newspapers, and a capital selection of magazines and periodicals —religious, social, and political. This institution fills long experienced void in the educational agencies of the town, and there is no doubt that its advantage will be fully _recognised by the poorer part of the population. The reading room opens at 9-30 a.m., and closes at 10 p.m, on week days, with the exception of Christmas Day and Good Friday. It will be closed on Sundays. , ALLEGED EXTENSIVE THEFT OF COPPER AT

WIDNES , At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Owen Kerley and Thomas Smith, of Widnes' and Patrick Hanlon, of War- rington were charged with having on or about the 2nd inst. stolen 495 lbs.bil copper worth £9 from a wagon on the Loudon and North-Westere Railway. George Christopher Howard. marine store dealer, Warrington, was charged with having received the stolen copper.—Mr. A. Browne defended Howard.—The evidence adduced showed that on the let inst. 356 ingots of copper were dermatched to the West Bank Dock, Widnes, from the works of the St. Helens Copper Company. When the ingots were counted on arrival at their destination, feur were missing. On the evening of the let inst. Kerte. asked Alfred Mercer, a carter, who lives at 7, Davis-street, Widnes, if he would take him four bars Of iron to Warrington, and Mercer agreed to do se. Next morning, at half-past five, he went to put his horse in the cart, and found that Smith and Kerley were there and had already put the load on the cart. These men accompanied Mercer to Warrington, where the latter discovered that he had been conveying sot iron, but blocks of copper.—W. Warburtlp, fitter's labourer, employed as assistant to the prisoner Howard's father,,deposed that on Thursday morn- ing, the 3rd lest., Kerley 'went to Howard's premises, and spoke to the risoner Howard, who afterwards directed War- button to accompany Kerley, which he did to a shop in King-street, where there were four blocks of copper. These were put in a wagon, and taken to the works of Messrs. Monks Hall, and Company. where they sheared them into pisces. Warburton was promised a sovereign for doing this work. On returning to the marine store, Warburton asked the prisoner Howard what he must do with the copper, and Howard replied that he could do what he liked with it, and he tipped it into a a field. On the following Tuesday Howard said "we will go. and shift that copper now," and after it tad been placed in a cart Howard drove away. On the Saturday previous Howard gave lam a sovereign, half a sovereign, and some silver, telling him to pay Kerley, whom he would find at Market•gate. He did so. Kerley did not give him the sovereign he promised, but Howard did.—ln reply to Mr. Browne. Warburton said he did not know the copper had been previously refused by Howard's father. The 356 trio not lent him to buy the copper for himself—Mr. Browne admiMd that his client bad sold the copper to Messrs Newell and Barker, machinists, Warrington, but contended that he did so on behalf of Warburton, who, he said, ought to be placed in the dock in place of Howard. On the sp. plication of Inspector Wood the prisoners were remanded. for a week. Howard was admitted to bail, himself in £4e, and two sureties of £2O each.

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNUAL REPORT.
div.p: MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNUAL REPORT.

Dr. Adams, medical officer of health, submitted hie annual report, which was a very voluminous one. In it be stated that the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority included the whole of the Runcorn Union, with the exception of Runcorn. proper, and under the Divided Parishes Acts contained 3fi townships, with 45,941 acres; the census population in 1881 was 18,892, and as estimated to the middle of 1886, it was 20,170. Daring the year ending December 31, 1886 s 620 births and 344 deaths were registered as havi.,g occurred within the rural district. Out of that total 26 formed the subject of coroners' inquest., while six were returned as uncertified;lt no medical attendant." The birth rate for the year was 30 7 per 1,000 of the estimated population. corn, pared with a birth rate of 284_ per 1,000 in 1885. ef 299 in. 1884, and of 312 in 1883. The death rate was 17.05 per. 1,000 of the estimated population, compared with a death rate of 194 in 1885. of 18.1 in 1884, and of 17.5 in 1883. The. year ended presented, in regard to the especial domain, of zymotic diseases, a marked improvement, compared with any other year for which be had reported. Smallpox did not make an appearance, and, he was glad to say, had net been in the district at all duriag his tenure of offne. Measles only appeared in the district during March and November, and was only answer.ble for one death. This was in marked contrast with 1885. when the disease was discovered in 273 houses, with 523 cases, resultirde in 38 deaths. Scarlet fever had appeared in five different town... abips, 'affecting six houses, with eight cases and two deaths. Diptheria had appeared at Strettoo, lickwick, and Fred.. abam, causing one death, which occurred at the tatter place. Three deaths had occurred from croup, one at BAlton, on at Helsby, and one at Budworth. Whooping cough was, responsible for four deaths—one each at flatten,. F'rodsham,. Kingwood, and Appleton. There had been no case of typhus fever, and the district had been Comparatively free from typhoid ; there had been twelve cases of tbe latter an& three deaths. It was a matter of regret that the death.raie should have been swollen during 1886 by IT deaths from Mat-Hama and, dysentery. To this total Frodsham contributed 8, seven of which occurred in persons under five years. Tie doctor added that be was of opinion that the erratic= feeding of infants contributed greatly to this result, 8& milk, among the working population, was a great rarity in rural districts. Children were brought up on smetened bread and water, or upon some kind of Crimea. poison. When, be asked, would mothers learn that mill-., was the natural food for the toothless babe, and that, failing to peol dime IL themselves, they should imitate as closely as pose sible that natural food? The incidence of deaths from this cause was distributed as follows :—Halton 1, Frodsharn 8„ Predsham Lordship 1, Kingsley 1, Sutton 1, Appleton 1, Dutton 2. Keckwick 1, and Whitley Superior 1. Two deaths oecerred from rheumatic fever, ate at Balton and one ak Weston. At the end of the year there wore no cases of scarlet fever or measles; one Case of typhoid fever was convalescent, and whooping cough appeared to be dying out. Speaking generally the district wes in a satisfa,ctory condition, one of the chief defects being the question of letter supply. The report also contained many mat- ters of interest, and it was decided that c- pies of it should, be printed, This was the principal business.

div.head: NOT BY EDGAR ALLAN POE?
div.p: NOT BY EDGAR ALLAN POE?
Once upon a midnight dreary, 111 in bed quite weak aid
wears,. With e eeplesseess, lone spirits, and indigestion sore ; While I strove In vain at napping, suddenly there cane a
tapping, As of some • ne gently rapping--rapning at my chamber door " It's Doctor Draughts," I muttered, "tapping atrmy cham- ber &Ara. _ . .
'Twas the Doctor, nothing more.

Oh ! distinctly I remeraber ; 11 was in the bleak December, And in every single member of my body pains I bore Eagerly I wished the morrow, vainly had I sought to borrow From drugs surcease of sorrow—sorrow for my pains galore; And I asked If I should ever beta healthy as before; Quoth the Doctor—" Nevermore " Your chest is bad, that's certain; your neuralgia's always hurting, And your liver Is so sluggish that life's to you a bore : And your heart's so bad at boating that in vain you're sleep _
entreating. _ While from weakness even now yon perspire from every pore"— rut, Doctor. when shall I be tlt te pass the threshold of my door?"

MANCHitsvaa ItAtitHMS.-Runcorn journeyed to Rusholme on Saturday to play the Rangers, bat were without the services of Lewis and Wainwright, reserves having to be called upon at the last moment to fill their places. Owing to the heavy fall of snow the ground was in wretched condition, making it almost impossible for the men to keep on their feet, and causing the ball to be very greasy and heavy. W. ughes kicked off, Robinson re- turning. Gatley and IV, ,aghes caused ,play to be located within the Rangers' 25. Herbert Hasleham then ran well, but was stopped by Woods, whereupon Broady, Wright, sod Barns dribblea back to neutral ground, Andrews further im- proving matters for Runcorn, being finally tackled by Par- kinson. Davies then obtained the ball, and rounding all his opponents scored a try, which was not improved upon. Robinson followed up the drop out and passed to Mee, who was brought down by Speakman. H. Hughes and Andrew& were here called upon to stop serveral rushes, and in the end Sabin got hold and gained a try for the Rangers, but the major point was not obtained. Broady spoilt the re- turn from the drop-out, Wright, W. Hughes. and Clarke dribbling on. This was, however, neutralized by Harrison and Pollard. Severe scrimmaging now took place in the Runcorn 25, and after some stiff work, Broady, W. Hughes, Wright, and Gatley got the ball away. Hasleham gained grouud for his side, and parting w tin the ball Cowley ob- tained it and punted to Parkinson, whose return was frus- trated by Clarku and Barns. H. Hughes next took up the offensive, and on Speakman receiving the ball from his captain a transfer was made to Davies, who gained his second try in beautiful style, Broady taking the place kick with success. The remainder of the game was not of an interesting character, with the exception of a good attempt at goal by Speakman. Eventually Runcorn won by 1 goal, 1 try, and 2 minor points. to 1 try and 3 minor poitats. Team—Runcorn: Woods. back; Davies, Speakman, and Cawley, threequarter back; H. Hughes (captain) and Andrews, half backs ; Wright, W. Hughes, Broady, Faulkner, Clarke, Gatley, Barns, Ford, and Other, for- wards. Manchester Rangers: Hammond, back; Sabin, Parkinson, and Ratcliffe, threequarter backs; Harrison and Taylor, half backs: H. Haslebam (captain), Harry Hasle- ham, Mee, Pollard, Hamnett, Robinson, Wilson, Jones, and Barron, forwards. %VEST LANCASHIRE CUP COMPETITION. WARSINGTON V. WIDNES.

The meeting of the Warrington and Widnes teams in the second round of the West Lancashire Cup Competition, which was looked forward to with each intense interest by local footballers, took place on Saturday on the Warrington ground. There was, as had been anticipated. a great con- course of spectators, something like 10,000 being present Special trains were ran from Widnes, both on the L. ea N W. and the Cheshire Lines Railways, and on the former there was also a special from St. Helens. Long before the time for starting, the large grandstand was crowded, and the square completely encircled by spectators, and before pro- ceedings commenced, every available point from which the play could be seen, and many from which it could be seen only imperfectly, was taken up. There was a good staff of c eastables present, under the command of Chief-Constable Hunt, and Inspectors Spinks and Cox, but throughout the spectators behaved in a most exemplary manner, notwith- standing the great excitement that prevailed. It had been rather anticipated that some disorder mieht ensue owing, to the feeling aroused in connection with the last match be- twersn the two teams, but as stated already, nothing of the sort occurred beyond a preliminary hooting of Farrell as he stepped on to the ground. The ground, it should be men- tioned, owing to the previous night's fall of snow, was very soft, and rather operated against good play, and the wea- ther was very cold: As usual, Frank Turner kicked off for Warrington, and Howard, who secured the ball, was brought down by Jolley. Speakman, Antrobus, and Massey showed up early in the game and Widnes were beginning to be pressed when Par- kinson, by a long kick, transferred the game into the War- rington half, but Appleton turned into touch. From a sub- sequent scrimmage, Fair Turner obtained hold and pat in a strong run. but passing forward, the ball was carried into touch in the Widnes half. The Wideesians by strong for- ward play now got the ball into the Warrington half, but the home Learn made a good defence, and the ball was soon transferred to the Widnes half, where Barnes having se- cured. he put in a abort run, but was brought down at the half Mg. By a tine dribble by Kiddie, Hardman and Smith, the Widnes men entered the Warriagten quarter, where Barnes relieved by a short kick. The ball was charged down, and from a scrimmage Piumpton put In a long kick, and the ball fell dead behind the Warrington posts. On the ball beitig kicked out by Frank Turner Parkinson returned, and a scrimmage brought the Widnes men in front of the Warrington goal. Plumpton passed the ball to Pennington, but missing, Jolley pounced upon the ball and landed it into touch. Jolley followed up his success by a long kick, which brought the ball to midfield. From a scrimmage Smith led through with a splendid dribble, and succeeded in passing the home backs, and landed the ball over the line. Plumpton fol- lowed up swiftly, but lost the ball, and it fell dead. On the ball being brought out, some good play by Massey trans- ferred the game to the Widnes territory. Widnes now had to withstand the pressure of a strong and combined attack, and owina tea miss by Pennington, who allowed the ball to pass under him, Warrington were within an ace of scoring and were only robbed of a try when they were close to the line by a timely kick of Bingham, which sent the ball Into touch. For some moments the game rested among thc for- wards, and nothing but scrimmages took place until Jolley showed up in a dodgy ran. Widnes relieved the pressure by a forward rush, but Barnes prevented any progress, and 1 returned the ball into the vieitora' half. Plumpton obtain- ing a free kick, landed the ball at centre flag, where a seams of scrimmages gave no advantage to either side until Speak- man obtained a free kick, fro n which the ball rolled into touch in the Widnes half. Farrell relieved by a strong kick, which placed the game In midfield. From this point Kiddie, Howard, and Woods made a fine dribble, aid carried the game into the Warrington quarter, where Appleton, by smart play, saved the game at a critical moment, by carry- ing the ball into touch. By a mistake Plumpton kicked the ball towards his own lines, but Bingham saved by fol- lowing up and kicking the ball into touch. Pennington improved matters by a splendid run, but was brought down in his own half. Jolley now showed up in fine form by a capital run, in which he dodged the whole of the visitors' forwards, and reached across the field before he was brought I down. Half-time was afterwards called, leaving the game as follows :—Widnes, two points; Warrington nil. On I change of ends, Kiddie kicked off for Widnes, and the ball I was returned by Frank Turner. Plumpton kicked back, but Ashton cleverly charged the ball down, and Pennington saved the game by getting in his kick, leaving the ball at centre flee,. Plumpton got in a good kick, and trans'erred the game to the Warrington half, and Howard managed to run ever, but the referee's whistle had been blown. Rigby and the brothers Turner afterwards carried the game Int* the Widnes half, where the visitors had to repulse a strong and combined attack. Farrell and Pennington played a splendid saving game, and Parkinson, by a free kick, af- forded some relief by kicking into touch in the Widnes half. Warrington followed up their attack, and Jolley getting hold made a splendid attempt to score. When he entered , the Widnes quarter he passed to Speakman, who was brought down. Warrington continued their attack, and Massev,securing the ball, was within an ass of the line when Bingham brought him down. Widnes having brought the ball out, Speakman secured and passed to Massey, but the latter missed, and the ball went into touch. From the line out Barnes secured and made a splendid at- tempt at goal, the ball falling barely six inches outside the cost. On the ball being brought out Widnes were again placed on the defensive, and Warrington invaded the visi- tors' lines in a strong attempt to score. They were several times on the point of scoring, and Davies had, in fact, reached tbe line when he was brought down. From a line- out Smith for Widow] relieved by a strong ran, but Barnes having secured made another attempt at goal, but it failed, and the ball went dead, the score being two points each. Plampton brought out, but owing to off-side play a scrim- mage was ordered in the Widnes half. From a scrimmage Massey made another attempt at goal dropping, the ball, however, hitting the post, and falling into play, Jolley ob- tained possession and rushed over the liae amid enthusiastic cheering. Speakman's attempt at goal was not a success. On the ball being brought out, Warrington contiened the pressure and from a scrimmage Massey obtained bold and , kicked the ball dead. On the ball being brought out, Frank Turner returned and Hardman obtained a free kick. Messey secured but was collared id the Widnes half by Farrell. Povey and Davies led a dribble through the scrimmage, when Pennington saved. The Widnes forwards now suc- ceeded in relieving for a short time, bat Littlewood follow- ing the ball from a side by Ashton, Widnes were again placed on the defensive. For a moment they succeeded in shaking eff their opponents and again entered the Warring- ton half, but they failed to make any permanent impression, and some strong play on the part of the home forwards placed the game in critical proximity to Widnes lines. Speakman passed to Massey, who made a good attempt at goal, the Dan Only falling on the outside of the post, and another dead ball was registered to the home team. The Visitors were now penned in their own quarter, Farrell even- tually being compelled to touch down. On the ball being brought out, the visitors displayed a fine passing game. and Plumpton by a strong run entered Warrington territory be- fore he was stepped. Play continued here for a few mi- nutes, when Warrington again forced the visitors back into their own ground. Time was then called and War- rington were declared the winners by nine points to two.

The home team were victors, after a hard fought game, by two goals to one. NOTES BY THE WAY. As we predicted last week. Warrington managed to come out of their encc unter with Widnes with a few points to the good. It must be said, however, that the match was rather more one-sided than had been anticipated, as after the first half Widnes fell away completely. That the score of the winners was not heavier was ;due to ' hard luck, for several times they were within an ace of scoring heavily. No doubt had Gilbert and the brothers Dillon been present Warrington would have done better still, though it must be sonfessed the play of the substitutes was everything that could be wished. Antrobne, in particular, has made a name for himseif, and WAS afflicted with the honour of being car- ried off the field by the spectators. But still when men have played together nearly the whole of a season they , naturally know the ways of the team better than fresh mea in their position. It was a good thing for the Warrington club that Turner i was not called upon to play for the county on Saturday, as 1 he was of great advantage, especially in the line out. Jolley ' certainly did not seem to be any the worse for being hurt, 1 and some noted critics say that he was the best man on the field. We only hope he may exhibit the Same form to- day against Wigan. Lack of organisation was the great factor in the defeat of the chemicals, and they will never show their true form until there is some master mind amongst them that can mould them. Perhaps Stoddart, the international three- quarter, who is about to take a situation in the town, will take them in hand.

NEW BOOKS, &c. " English Writers" is the simple title of a most important work which is being issued by Messrs. Cassell and Co. It is nothing less than a history of our literature, although it is modestly described as "An attempt towards a history of English Litera- ture by Henry Morley, L L.D., professor of Englieh Literature at University College, London." It is over twenty years since Professor Morley issued a volume of 801110 Soo pages giving "an account of the writers before Chaucer, with an introductory sketch of the Four Periods of English Literature." He speaks of this by no means insignificant work as part of the fulfilment of a young desire ; but the wider know- ledge and riper experience which he has gained dur- ing the past twenty years have led him to recast the original design. It is now proposed to tell the story of Euglish Literature in twenty half-yearly volumes; the whole narrative will be continuous ; the book, one. The first volume is bef,.re us, and it is emi- nently satisfactory as an introduction to the series. The introduction itself extends over ion pages, and it is a rapid but comprehensive survey of the chief features of our literature. Book I proceeds to deal with the forming of the people, old literature of the Gael, the Cymry, and of the Teutons, while other chapters are devoted to Scandinavia, the poem of "Beowulf," and the fight at Finnesburg. The vol- ume is exhaustively indexed, and as this admirable arrangement will be continued, each section of this gigantic work may be regarded as complete in itself. Book II is to be issued due log the summer, and will cover the period from Casdmon to the Conquest. After the foretaste which Professor Morley has provided, it will be looked forward to with eagerness by readers of all classes, and especially by students of literature. , Messrs. Camelia are to be commended for their enterprise in undertaking the publication of this snag- Slum opus. "The Influence of Clothing on Health" is the title of an exceedingly useful work also published by Messrs. Cassell. It is from the pen of Mr. Frederick Preves, surgeon and lecturer on anatomy at the London Hos- pital. The writer believes in the beautiful as well as the useful in matters of dress; but he naturally gives the first place to the preservation of health in advocat- ing certain materials and styles of clothing. The illustrations go to show that the results of tight- lacing and tight boots are thh reverse of beautiful, while the effects on health are of the most disastrous , kind. Every portion of dress, for males and for females, is fully considered; and he must be an ex- ceedingly stupid sort of person who is not influenced for good by the perusal of Mr. Treves' book. Those who like to study a question from its scientific eide will find plenty of statistics to support the theories set forth; but the question is for the most part treated in a style to bring it home to the general reader. The work is neatly bound in cloth and is published at 25. The " Life of Dickens " is the current issue of the " Great Writers " series, which is being published by Mr. Walter Scott, Lo idon. It is written by Mr. Frank T. Marzials ; and, as might be expected, it is a most readable book. The story of the life of Dickens is well told, and the reader is treated to a considerable amount of thoughtful criticism of the viorks of the great novelist. Thera is a good index, and a complete bibliography by Mr. J. P. Anderson, of the British Museum—and all for one shilling. " Longfellow's Prose Works,'' published by the same firai, is amongst the Camelot Classics. There are many who are familar with Longfellow as a poet who know nothing whatever of him as the author of the two stories, "Hyperion " and "Kavanagh." Both of these tales are given in this volume, besides the poet's papers on " The Trouveres " and "The Devotional Poetry of Spain." There is an excellent introduction by Mr. William Tirebuck, who adds in- terest to the works which follow by showing, with sympathetic insight, how far they may be regarded as autobiographical. The dainty series of the Canterbury Poets is en- riched this month by "The Poems of Sydney Dobell (selected), with an introductory memoir." This is jag such in issue as is needed for the masses, who have heard little or nothing of this sweet singer. It is not every reader who can afford a complete copy- right edition ; but the name is legion of those who are willieg to spend a shilling on a well-printed and neatly-bound volume of ilden verse. " Last Year's Leaves" is the title of a small volume of verse published by Mr. Walter Scott. The author, Mr. John Jervis Beresford, MA. is, we gather, a Welshman, who is justly fond of his native land, for he seems most happy when versifying its legends. His style is chastened and refined; but somehow when the reader is most expectant, he finds himself most doomed to disappointment. Mr. Beresford is strongly imbued with piety, and has a good word to say for Church and State. He is a Tory and a Poet—a novel conjunction as it will seem to most people. Tbe book is tastefully bound, and it is well. printed on toned paper. "Triumphant Democracy, or Fifty Years' March of the Republic," is haying a large sale, as published by Messrs. Sampson, Low, and Co. The author, Mr. Andrew Carnegie, seems to have written the work as a tribute of affection to the country of his adoption ; and he certainly sings its praises as a lover. We are continually hearing, directly or indirectly, of the ex- traordinary progress which is being made in the United States; but when the sum total is put before us in black and white it looms so large as to almost take away one's breath. And yet Mr. Carnegie is not given to exaggeration. However playful or fanciful he may be at times in his way of putting his ease, it must be admitted that be is always in one form or another backed up by solid facts. We in this country have been accustomed for generations to speak of our- selves as the greatest manufacturers and as the richest people in the world; but we have been passed in both respects by the United States. Details of facts of this kind have a tendency to knock the conceit out of the Britisher, but at the same time they ought to stimulate him also to "go ahead." "Triumphant Democracy" is racily written; it is full of information, and, as it is nowhere dull, we can quite understand why it has been so favourably received. It is to be hoped it will be carefully read by Democrats at home; it points the way they must follow in very many things, "The Tale of Troy" (Messrs. Macmillan and Co.), is a new rendering of an old story "done into Eng- lieh by Aubrey Stewart, M.A." This is just the book to put into the hands of scholars when it is desired that they should be charmed into acquaintance with the classical details of the war between the Greeks and the Trojans without running risk of contact with the gramma which marks the literal translation, Kr.

The display of last Saturday has given the supporters of the Warrington team a pretty strong feeling of confidence in their ability to "polish off" Wigan to-day. We think 1 they will do this, barring accidents, but accidents sometimes happen, and, besioes, Wigan is not a team to be treated lightly. It has sometimes been remarked of the cupholders that they have a tendency to take matters easy at the open- ing of a game, and last Saturday gave an instance in point. Having got into the semi-final of a cup tie, it is necessary to strain every nerve from the beginning, and if Warrington , do this to-day we anticipate they will come out with a few points in hand. Our readers will be glad to hear that besides securing fresh home and home fixarres with Broughton and Wake- field Trinity, Mr. Warren, the energetic secretary of the Warring,ton Club. has been successful in arranging fixtures with Halifax, lately the holders of the Yorkshire Challenge Cop. We also hear that be has arranged with Kendal Hornets, who, by the way. beat Swinton a short time ago, , the match with the Kendal Town Club being played on the following Monday. Runcorn maintained their unbeaten record on Saturday, but they had by no means an easy task to defeat that rising Manchester organisation the Rangers. Certainly they were without several good forwards, and the field, which had evi- dently not long since been need for agricultural purposes, wage series of furrows, awkward for strangers to navigate, whilst the "upper crust" was terribly aoft and sloppy. These are two circumstances which made it almost impose foible to play the fast loose game that Runcorn usually do. However, with unselfish passing, and Davies In champion running form, the "red tails" came away victorious. Harry Speakman had hard lines for a dropped goal. The matches in the second round of the competition for the West Lancishire Challenge Cup were all brought off succeasfully on Saturday. The following is a summary of I the results, viz. :—Warrington beat Widnes at Warrington ilrr a try and five minors, to two minors; Aspull beat St. 'alone Recreation by three tries and seven minors, to four minors, at Avail ; Wigan beat Walkden by one goal two tries and two minors, to one goal, at Walkden ; and Tyldes- ley beat Walton by three goals and five minors, to one minor, at Walton. The draws for the semi•finals were made on Saturday night, with the result ;bat Warrington and Wigan will meet to-day on the ground of the St. Helens Recreation. The umpires will be Meer. Trevors-Smith and T. Kneen and the referee Mr. W. H. Wallace (Cheshire county), or Mr. A. T. Kemble (Liverpool.) The other con- test still be between Aspull and Tyldesley, at Wigan. The 'umpires in this case will be Messrs. Beswick (Swinton) and Hickson (Old Boys), and the referee Mr. Duranda (Liver- pool.) Two important matches were brought off at Kennington Oval on Saturday, one being between Lancashire and Mid- dlesex County teams, and the other, under Association rules, between Preston North End and the Corinthians. There was a great crowd of spectators, amongst them being H R.H. the Prince of Wales, the proceeds of the matches going in support of the Imperial Institute. In the Aseocia• tion game each side scored a goal, while in the Rugby Lan- cashire won by a try to two min ws. The team which re- presented Lancashire in the Rugby game was compesed as follows: S Roberts (Swinton), back. J Valentine (Swin- ton), J Robertson (Broughton Rangers), and V &ter (Sal- f6rd), threequarter backs; J H Payne (captain, Broughton), and J Mille (Swinton), half backs ; C Anderton (Manchester Free Wanderers), H C Chapman (Liverpool Old Boys), H Eagles (Salford), A T Kemble (Liverpool), F MOSS (Brough- ton), R Seddon (Broughton Rangers), J W Roberts (Sal- ford), Stockly (Liverpool), and A Teggin (Broughton Rangers), forwards. Representative team of Ireland and Wales, under both Rugby and Association rules also met on Saturday. The Rugby champions met at Birkenhead Park, and a stiffly contested game was the result, ending in a victory for Wales by one goal, one try, and four minor (points to three tries. The Association game was brought off at Belfast, and in this case, Ireland asserted its superiority by four goals to one.
