The War Office has decided to use 1,000 carrier pigeons at the Easter manceuvres..

Snow again fell heavily in Manchester on Wednesday, end also in matey other i3art 5 of the country. The Scotch authorities have forbidden the importation of Irish cattle owing to the prevalence of disease in that country. Lady Brooks opened a bazaar on Wednesday at Black- burn in aid of the building fund of St. Peter's Church, Salisbury. A telegram from Mob ill, Ireland, reports that a railway accident occurred there on Tuesday night, in which three persons were killed and four severely injured. T.RIP1:11 NIII&DBR tr; PARIS.—A Reuter's telegram from Paris said that a lady, named Regnault and her two maid- servants were murdered on Wednesday night in the Rae Montaigne.

ST. Jouts's CROWE CRoia.—A concert and enter- tainment of an inte,esting character was given in the Dis- trict Infants' Scoool, Market-street, Earlestnwn, on Mon- day night, the proceeds of which were to be devoted to the ahoir picnic fund. Mrs Thacker and Miss Thacker (organ- ist of bt. John the Baptist's Church) had charge of the arrangements, and a programme of vocal and instrumental music was rendered. The attendance was large. The se- lections included pianoforte duets and solos, songs, recita- tions, and a dramatic performance entitled " Honeymoon experiments." Those who took part in the eyao.ning's enter- tainment were Mrs rhacker, Miss 'I hacker, IMss Matthews, Miss Shaw, Miss A. K Wood, Mien Brett.,lle, Miss C Jack. son, Miss Thrnes, and lktessrs W Greaves, Williams, W Jackson, G Jackson. &c. At the close of the entertainment the members of the choir and a few friends enjoyel them- selves for a abort time in dancing.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF
GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at flee Workhouse, on Wednesasy morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Harrison, Blackhurst, Jolley, Jones Voisey, Heaton, Greening, J. Houghton, Gibson, Brown, Owen, Derbyshire, Isherwood, Balharry, Humphries, Clarke, Ratcliffe, Wright, W. Houghton, Hibbert, Strange, Eckersley, Swinton, Grange, Pennington; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assis- tant clerk).

div.head: PADOATH SCHOOLS.
div.p: THE PADOATH SCHOOLS.

It was stated in the minutes of Tha..S,;bools Committee that the doctor had reported the general health of the chil- dren to be good.—On the motion of the Caernitaw, seconded by Mr. ISHERWOOD, the minutes were confirmed.

div.head: SCHOOL VSXS.
div.p: SCHOOL VSXS.

The School Fees Committee 'reported that fees had been allowed in 86 Cd3oB, 80 of which were old and six new cases. —On the motion of Mr. BROWN, fldCouded by Mr. JOLLY, the minutes were carried. VACCINATION AT NEWTON.

The CLERIC said a letter had been -received from Mr. Cooper, vaccination officer at Earlestown, with reference to matte's connected with the Newton registrar, and complain- ing that be was by these interfered with in the discharge of his duties. He kthe clerk) was afraid the registrar would Pot into trouble, as an inspector bad been over from London the other day. He suggested that the letter should be referred to the Newton Relief Committee, who could have the registrar and Mr. Cooper before them.—This suggestion was adopted.

div.head: TlLlif EXPEND ITTJ RH.
div.p: TlLlif EXPEND ITTJ RH.

With regard to the expenditure the CLERK read the fol- lowing statement:—" The estimate of contribtations required from the various townships in the Union for the half .year ending at September, 1887, has formally been submitted to your Board. The call made at Michaelmas last was for £10,123, making, with a balance then in hand of £2,082, a total capital for the present half-year of £12,205. The esti- rested expenditure to the close of the half-year was as fol- lows: Separate charges £lBB. common charges £8,384, county rates £2,290, total £10,842, leaving in the treasurer's hands an estimated balance of £1,363. The estimate your Board are now invited to approve provides £lBB for separate charges. £7,748 common charges, £2,247 county rate, and £1,290, the useral proportion to meet expen- diture before another call can be made, the total prob- able outlay for the half-year ending Michaelmas, 1887 e being £11,471. Deducting the £1,363 from this aura leaves the actual contribution now to be fixed £lO,lOB. The actual cost of maintenance in the corresponding half of last year was £2,111 4e 11d, and a sum of £2,150 is propcsed to be now provided. Out relief in the same period amounted to £2,178 7s 100, and provision is now made for £2,100. there being signs of reduction under this head. For lunatic /account a sum of £1,200 is fixed, compared to an actual expenditure in the corresponding half of last year of £1,122. Na material variance from expenditure under other heads is evidenced, corresponding sums are therefore fixed upon. There cal be no reasonable doubt that the sums thus to be provided will amply meet the outlay in the half-year, and it may also reasouahly be hoped that a substantial balance to the credit of the Union will result at its close, the out- look bearing a more satisfactory character than it had a year ago.—Pn the motion of Mr. BLACKSII7RST, seconded by Mr. JOLLEY, the rev:l,n was adopted.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF THE MASTER.
div.p: THE RESIGNATION OF THE MASTER.

With regard to the rEcent resignation of the Workhouse Master, the following two resolutions were passed, viz.:— "'that as the services of Mr. and Mrs Mackey will by order of the Local Government Board, be determined on the 26th inst., the Guardians direct that all hooks, papers, docu- ments, furniture, property, and other tffects in the posses- sion of Mr. and Mrs Mackey as master and matron, be given up by theni on that day to Mr. Brown as chairman of the House Committee, and that facilities be given to Mr. Mac- key to make up and complete his books to that date for audit at Mr. Harbourne's office."—" 1 hat from and after the 26th inst., Mr. Harbourne be requested to give as much attention as his duties will allow to the supervision of the workhouse inmates, and to compliance with the ordinary duties of master until the master and matron to be selected undertake their duties."

div.head: Tll3l TENDERS.
div.p: Tll3l TENDERS.

The half-yearly tenders to supply the Union with pro- visions &c. were considered and the following accepted : Butcher's meat, Mr. John Cross ; bread, Mr. Roberts; Pen- maerimawr stone, Warrington Slate Company ' • coal and slack, Messrs. Evans: coffins, Mr. Wells cord and twill, Messrs. Unsworth ; meal and flour, Mrs. Eckorsley ; fire- wood, Mr. W. Heaton; fish, Mrs. Lawless; milk (schools) Mr. Joseph Houghton; (workhouse) Mr. James Warbur- ton ; dr ,pery, Mr. Fietcher ; beer and porter, Messrs. J. & T Uregory, Prescot ; clogs, Mr. Jones; straw, Mr. James Warburton; brushes, Mr. Chester; glass, Messrs. Gaskell and son; shaving, Mr. John Stock; shoes, Messrs. Rob- erts and Sons. The tenders for groceries, leather, and carbolic soap were left over to be dealt with lay the House Committee. THE APPOINTERNT OF MASTER AND MATRON.

The business of appointing a new master and matron of the workhouse in place of Mr. and Mrs. Mackey was next proceeded with. In all there had been 59 applications for the vacant offices, many of the app,icants already holding appointments in connection with other Unions, either as masters of workhouses, relieving officers, or porters, /to. There were also a master and matron of a reformatory, the governer and matron of a poor-house, a builder, a schoolmaeter and schoolmistress, an hotel manager, an ex.ebip captain, a harness maker, a Board school master, and matron, a superintendent and matron of an idiot asy- lum, a farm steward, a wire worker, a bookseller. an indus- trial trainer, and a captain of the Royal Scots Fusilier. Among other places applications belong-d to Warrington, Liverpool, Kirkham, Fylde, Builth, Brecknock, Whitby, 'Salford. Bristol Loughborough. Aberdeen, Bolton, Dews- bury, Chelsea, Huddersfield, Romford, Essex, Leicester, Rugby, Westbnrron-Severn, Gloucestershire, Biggleswade, Belford, Rawtenstall, Chorlton, Norfolk, Doncaster, Rut. land, Conway, Glossop, Pontardawe, near Swansea, Exeter, Goole, Dartford, and Dumfries. Out of the N applicants the following had been selected at a private meeting of the Board, and requested to attend the ordinary meeting on Wednesday, namely :—John Bray and Emily Brewer Bray, master and matron, Wisheach, Cambridge; William T. Overstay and Eliza Oversby, relieving officer and wife, Liverpool; Thomas and Jane Knight, master and matron, Loughborough, Leicestershire; John and Edith Ashwood, master and matron, Westbury-on-Severn ; Charles Harrell Ward and Mary Ward, master and rnatren, Doncaster; and James and Ann Elizabeth Graham, master and matron, Goole, Yorkshire. • It Was stated by the Clerk that since the selection of the half-dozen candidates he had received a letter from Mr. Knight, one of those selected, withdrawing his application as.he had obtained an increase of salary from his own Board of Guardians. The other applicants who were all present, were brought into the Board room separately, and several questions were pot and answered. A vote we, then r taken as to the appointment, with the result that Charles Harrell Ward and Mary Ward were appointed by a large majority.

div.head: -PROPOSED MONEY GRANT TO MRS._ MACKEY.
div.p: -PROPOSED MONEY GRANT TO MRS._ MACKEY.

Mr. VOISZY moved the following resolution :—" That the Guardians are wishful in consideration of Mrs. Mackey's lengthened, honourable, and efficient services, and in sym- pathy for her unfortunate position of having to lose her appointment of Matron through the resignation of her hns- hand ; to make her a money grant on leaving the service of the Union; and that the Local Government Board be con- suited on the amount of what sum could or should be granted under the circumstances." He (Mr. Voisey) said that he submitted that resolution as an alternative course for personally be should have preferred if some arrange- ment could have been made for Mrs. Mackey to remain at the workhouse as matron, bet it seemed to be the general opinion of the Guardians that that course was impractic- able. If that resolution were passed it would be necessary to fix upon a sum that might be given to Mre. Mackey. The question then would be what the corn sbould be. On the new appointment of master and matron they would save £6O a year, and he should suggest that that amount might be voted to Mrs. Mackey for one or two years. (" Ne, no.") His proposition would be that they vote Mrs. Mackey twice .I:6o.—Mr. &Acton:am: You will not carry it, Mr. Voisey ; it would be better to put it in some other shape.— Mr. VOISEY said he wanted to bear the opinion of the Guardians; he did not want to propose any- thing that would meet with a direct nega- tive. Mr. Bow ly seconded Mr. Voisey's mo- tion. Mr. HARRISON had pleasure in supporting the motion. He supposed that if Mrs Mackey had had to retire from her situation because of illness or some other incapacity, she would have been quite within her right in applying for an annuity, and if that Board had chosen to vote her an annuity it would, subject to the approval of the Local Government Board, have been granted to her. He did not think she should be put in a worse position by reason of the unfortunate circumstance in connection with her hus- band. It would not, he thought, be now advisable to pro- pose that she have an annuity, and the only alternative was the grant of a sum of money,—Mr. DARBYSHIRB opposed the motion, and *expressed himself in favour of nothing whatever beieg granted to Mrs Mackey either as an annuity gratuity, or superannuation. He should like to say of the proposer of the motion (Mr. Voisey) that, when they got rid of the case of Mr. and Mrs Mackey, he would be some- thing like Othello—his occupation would be gone. (Laugh- ter.) The time Mr. Voisey had been on the Board it had been his business to defend Mr. and Mm Mackie whether right or wrong.—Mr. HARRISON I don't believe it; it is an improper remark to make.—Mr. DARBYSHIRB then went on to sav that Mr. Velsev stated that there had been no fault to find with the way Mrs Mackey had performed her duties. But they must remember that Mr. Voisey was a very young Guardian. How did he know,lwhen he was as a Guardian not a year eld ? It would have been better if some one who knew how the duties were performed had , taken the matter up, instead of one who only knew what he had been told by someone else. Mr. Derbyshire then re- ferred to difficulties which be said the Guardians formerly had in getting the washing done at the workhouse. It even became a bye-word in the town, and when people MIN Guar- dians going to the Board meeting they used to say" There goes the washer-women again." (Laughter.) When the children were at the barracks there was not the means for washing there, and the clout's were sent to the workhouse
M OLINEUX'S " CHECK-REPEATIM " PIANOS.

in a cart belonging to a man named Jarvis, but he was rent j back from the workhouse, and was kept travelling between the workhouse and the barracks. Jarvis was peid for the time it took him to take the clothes' and it did not matter to him how often he was sent back. (Laughter.) Mrs Mackey, in fact, refused to do the heavy washing for the children, although the Guardians said it must be don. at the Workhouse, and at length the Local Government Board was written to,-and they wrote requesting Mrs Mackey to perform the duties requested of her by the Guardians. The Guardians at the time were laughed at, and people said they could not manage the washerwomen. (Laughter.) That was one fault, but he (Mr Derbyshire) mirht mention others; but he mentioned that one simply because Mr Voisey said there bad been no fault found. Be was of opinioe that Mr ead Mrs Mackey had been quite sufficiently paid by the ratepayers during the time they had been at that Workhouse.—Mr W HOUGHTON said be had sympathy with Mr and Mrs Mackey. but be also had sym- pathy with the ratepayers. Mr and Mrs Mackey had been liberally dealt with by the Union He expressed disapproval of the motion.—Mr JOLLEY said his impression was that Mrs Mackey, with all the faults that had been heard, had been a very excellent matron, and they would be fortunate if they got a better one. ([fear, hear.) He should never agree to an annuitl, being granted, but he would be willing that Ms Mackey should be given a grant as a , recognition of her services.—Mr RATCLIFFE said if Mr and Mrs Mackey were really poor it would , I be right enough to make a grant, but if it was true that Mr. Mackey was a wealthy man, they had no right to vote away money to a wealthy man. Mr. Mackey had been there 15 or 20 years in a very good position—it must have been a good peeition, for he stuck to it like a leech. He would oppose the motion.—The CHAIRMAN said there were two or three things they should bear in mind. First of all they should bear in mind they were not proposing to vote their own money; they were proposing to vote the ratepayers' money. That the per- sons in question had admittedly fulfilled their duty—at least Mrs. Mackey had done so—to the satisfaction of a ma- jority of the Guardians was true, but there was another fact, and that was that they bad been well paid for fulfilling their duties. Another thing he would suggest to them was this: that they could not separate as between man and wife. Sup- posing they made a money grant they put themselves in the position of rewarding indirectly a man who had been called upon to resign his position. (Hear, hear.) He thought that that would be a false position to stand in. With regard to Mr. Derbyshire's remarks, he could only say that the facts were as Mr. Derbyshire had represented them to be.— Mr. VOIREY, in replying, said all he had said in favour of Mr. and Mrs. Mackey was said because he honestly felt they I were entitled to it. There had been every opportunity given to allege anything that might be alleged against Mr and Mrs Mackey, and he had never before heard a word about Mr. Derbyshire's soap and suds. That matter would be dealt with at the time, and probably Mr. Derbyshire was in the minority in the discussion at that time. He had acted towards Mr. Mackey as one man feeling honestly to- wards another to whom he felt there had been some unfair treatment shown. He still retained the feeling that the matter upon which he had been called to send in his resig- nation was a trivial matter' and there was also that feeling outside. He did not think the chairman's argument had all the force he wished to throw into it, seeing that the appoint- ments of Mr. and Mrs. Mackey were separate appointments. —Mr. HARRISON thought the chairman bad forgot about the Married Women's Property Act. ("Oh, oh," and laughter.)—The CHAIRMAN acid he did not wish to em- phasise any one fact for or against Mrs. Mackey. With re- gard to the statement of Mr. Voisey that certain charges had not previously been made against Mrs. Mackey, the Chairman remarked that the Board had tried to spare Mr. and Mrs. Mackey's feelings as much as possible.—A vote was then taken on Mr. Voiseyat motion, when it was re- jected by 17 votes to six. Those who voted in its favour were Messrs. Voisey, Brown, Harrison, Heaton, Jolley, and Isherwood. This was all the business of pnblic interest.

CABINET COIINCIL.—A Cabinet Council was held at the Foreign Wise at noon on Thursday. All the members, ex- cept Lord John Manners and Sir Michael Hicks-Beach,were present, and the Attorney-General (Sir Richard Web- ster) was in attendance during the sitting. Irish affairs, and mere particularly the proposed Bill dealing with lease- holders and evictions, were the main subjects ueder discus- sion.,

MR. GLADSTONE AND MR. CHAMBSRLAIN.—MT. Glad- stone dined with Mr. Chamberlain on Thursdny night. Several members of Parliament were among the pay, among them being one of pronounced Home Rule proclivi- ties. The invitation to the ex-Premier is one of long standing, but s veral circumstances have hitherto delayed its accept- ance. The gathering was purely a social one, and politics were eschewed.

Com:dirtEn FOR MIIRDER.—On Thursday, at Bury, Thomas Splaine, collier, was ckmmitted for trial for mur- dering Henry Manns, at Radcliffe, on January 29th Splaine's wife, John Birch, and George Kay were also nom., mitted as accessories. Mann was trying to protect a friend from being stabbed by Mrs. Splaine, and was dragged into the house and beaten about the head with a fire bar so savagely that be died on Wednesday.

div.p: FOURTEEN YEARS OF AGONY ENDED
FOURTEEN YEARS OF AGONY ENDED FOURTEEN YEARS OF AGONY ENDED

I have been afflteted for about fourteen years with an Obstinate skin oisesse balled by some oocton eczema, and others, psoriasis My body and bands were covered with Itching scabs, and during this time I have constant y used gloves. From South America, where I was for many years established, I have travelled through Spain. Portu- gal and France where I have consulted Beveral physicians of acknowlei gad celebrity, tried hundreds of remedies, not one having the least effect. My friends bare and else- where know that I have been a great sufferer, and that my condition at times has been such as to make me despair ,1 ever being able to find a cure or even a relief to my sick- ness. Last summer I again went to Paris, directly to the St. Louis Hospital, but instead of finding any cure I was % at death's dr. Military Examiner: "What must a man be to be buried with military.honours ?" Recruit: "Dead." " FAITHFUL ONES ' SHOULD PONDER THIS.—A boy described the heathen " folks wot don't fight over religion." THE VERY LATEST FAdi FOB NATURALISTS.—No horse ever found a mare* nest. The discovery can be made only by a donkey. Physician to convalescent: "You feel stronger now, do you not ?" Convalescent: "Oh, yea, doctor—very much stronger! I'm strong enough for almost any- thing." Physician: "Then I will send in my bill." We trust that no class of society will be offended if we express the hope that the time will come when trousers that bag at the knee 'will be in the height of fashion. _ . .

Francis Murphy, the temperance advocate, was asked his opinion about legislation against the liquor traffic, and said: "if legislation would save people Moses would have been the Christ." The experienced editor can always tell at sight the man who comes in with his first attempt at original poetry. He walks on tiptoe, and looks as though he had just passed a forged cheque or strangled a baby.: Master (to his apprentice after a drubbing: "It gives me real pain to thrash you so often." Apprentice: "Indeed I Pains you, does it? Then let's have another hiding." ' Warms's NAKED.—A room in a London club was once a studio a Watts, the artist, and the walls are still covered with huge and prominent *male figures. Lord Houghton is said to be responsible for the saying, "These afe not Watts's hymns, but Watts's hers." , BEGINNING! IN Tima.--L--" James, I don't see but what I shall have to have a new bonnet if I'm going to the Per- manent Exhibition with you." "Penn—why that's three or four years from now. You'd better read up." "0, yes, James, Ido read up. But three or four years I are none too long beforehand to begin if I am going to get the money nrtime. WILLING TO SCALE.—" Did you get diamonds for Christmas ?" she was asking in a Baker-street car. "Yes." "How much did they cost ?" "My husband says $350, but I haven't had a jeweller price them yet. My mind is made up to scale all the way from $350 down to $15." "That's right, Bertha. It may save you a great shock to your nervous system." HIS LITTLE Joxa—Mrs. Sardonicus—" I see here in the paper that the Irish children have to go barefooted in the winter. I think that's dreadful, don't you? " Sardonicus—" Why, not very. Igo barefooted at least a third of the time myself." Mrs. Sardonicus—" I just wish you'd tell me when you ever went barefooted in the winter time?" Sardonicus—" Why, Igo barefooted o' nights." LOST.—Father: "Well, Jennie, now you've had a first- class education, and I suppose you are ready to assume i the duties of a young woman n society. Oh, by the way, let roe see your diploma." Daughter: " I—l—l've lost it, father. It was burned up this morning by accident." Father: "Great Scott! Then I've spent all , that money for nothing!" I ." Pretty ? No, I won't say baby is pretty," declared a young mother, "for I can speak of him impartially, even though he is my own, and that's more than most mothers can do. He has lovely blue' eyes, perfect in shape; hair like the morning sunshine; mouth—well, no rosebud could be sweeter; complexion divinely fair; nose just too cunning for anything; in. fact, he's fault- less. But I won't say he's pretty." THE POET BORN BUT NOT ALTOGETHER "Fir."—" The poet is born, sir," said a man haughtily, as with a shake of the head he received a roll of manuscript from an editor. "Oh, is he ?" replied the editor, with a pleasant smile. "Well, when he gets old enough to write some- thing, tell him to come and see me. Good-bye "—and he resumed his labours. Gentleman who has lately presented his man-servant with a pair of badly-fitting trousers: "Johns when I wore those trousers myself, I thought they were very badly made indeed; but, now I swPiem on you. I •am disposed to think otherwise." John, intending to be complaisant: "Ou, I dare say! But there's some folk ne'er look well in ottything." The papers have given accounts of an aged cook who has just suceeeded to an income of somewhere about thirtyhousand pounds a year. Of course she has been intervrewed. The reporter was rather astonished when, in reply to his remark, " Ah, you will be able to keep a cook yourself now !" she answered ironically, "Not if I know it." That cook knows something. . .

A farmer's daughter during the rage for albums handed to Willis Gaylord, an American poet, an old account-book ruled for pounds, shillings, and pence, and requested a contribution. He happily utilised the figures as follows:—" This world's a scene as dark as Styx, Where hope is scarce worth 2s. ed. Our joys are borne so fleeting hence That they are dear at 18d; And yet to Stay here most are willing, Although they may not have a Is." Tizz DIVINE AFFLATI79.—A charming Sonthern lady devoted to wooing the muses lately had a call from a gentleman, but she sent a polite request to be excused on a plea of indisposition. trust she is not seriously ill; perhaps it's but a touch of the 'divine afflatus,' " he said, arising to depart. "Oh, no!" replied the mes- senger, thinking -the "divine afflatus" must be some terrible disease; "it's nothing dangerous; she Only has a cold!" • A warm-hearted Salvationist, whose wife died about a month since, began courting a "Happy Eliza" mill- girl immediately after his spouse's decease. The mill- girl reciprocated his tender attentions. This conduct so enraged the other daughters of Eve employed at the mill that they tried to cool the ardour of the loving pair by pelting and rubbing them with snow. The persecu- tion of these martyrs would make a good subject for a frieze, which might decorate one of " General" Booth's halls with advantage. Scene—Drawing-room of suburban villa: dramatis person&—A Couple of young ladies, bosom friends. "My dearest Nelly, I could not rest until I had come and made an effort to dispel the gloomy thoughts which, to judge from your letter of yesterday, threatened to develop into suicidal mania. 'Tis true Alfred has jilted you— the wretch !----still, try to act like a sensible girl, and look out for another to take his place." "Your advice comes too late, darling." "Good gracious, Nelly, you surely haven't taken poison !" "Well, n-n-no ; but the fact is; I—l became engaged again yesterday!" SomErruNe OF A STORY.—As an illustration of the "colossal liars" of the West, General Mc.Cook relates the following. He was travelling smolt the Rocky Mountains, and, straying one morning from the trail, stood for a moment entranced by the magnificent landscape spread before him, when he was aroused from his meditation by the footsteps of one of the guides, who had followed him lest he should lose his way. "Is not this magnificent, Bill?" exclaimed the General, anxious to share his delight. "It's mighty purty, Gineral," said the guide; "but I can show you bigger sights nor this. Why, one time Kansas Jim and me had been trampin' three days and nights, and we came to a plain, and right in the midst of it was a forest all turned to solid stun !" The General smiled and remarked, "I have heard of petrified trees before, Bill." The guide, without changing countenance, continued, "But that warn't all, Gineral; thar war a buffalo on that plain and he war petrified on the clean jump, and his hufs had kicked up a bit of sod, and I'm durnEd ef that warn't petrified in the air ! " The General turned an amused countenance on the narrator and said, "Why, Bill, the sod would have fallen to the ground by the force of gravity !" Without any hesita- tion, Bill answered, "But, Gineral, the gravity war petri- fied too !" •

Re then threatened to assault i.e—The -defendant had been previously convicted for assaulting hie wife, and he was now bound over to keep the peace for six I months. THE CURE OF HYDROPHOBIA. Sir,—Ttie frequent outbreaks of hydrophobia in various parts of the kiogdotn, and the knowledge that M. Pasteur's treatment only professes to be preventive, not curative, that disease, Induces me to ask von to make known to your large circle of readers the vapour bath treatment for hydro- phobia, so successfully practieed be the late Dr. Salmon, of Paris, and other eminent physicians. For the past eighteen months large sums of looney have been sp.nt in makin:: known all over the kingdom this treatment, not only as a preventive, but as a cure for the disease after it has set in, vet, for seine unexplained reason, people seem unwilling to give its trial. THE JUBILEE CELEBRATION IN WARRINGTON.] Sir —The report of the local meeting as to the celebra- tion Of the Queen's Jubilee, which you published last week, was very entertaining reading, and lam fare must have provoked the mirth of all thoughtful people. That oar sten of mark caw think of no snore rational way of celebra- ting a conspicuous historical event than by indulging in such childish amusements as processions and powder, passes comprehension. To me mind the only sensible proposition -(mitting aside the Free Library question, which our monied men won't see) was made by Mr. William Diggle, who sug- gested a Mechanics' Institute and Technical School. But Mr. Diggle seems to have been the only working-an at the meeting, and consequently got little consideration. I regret circumstances prevented me attending the meeting, or I should have been pleased to second the only prepohition- worth entertaining. No one knows better than Our manu- facturers how English goods are being beaten in consul ouence of our workpeople not having received a technical education, and yet they seem quite content to let the pre- sent unsatisfactory state ef things continue. As it is, these Warringtonians who desire to better their position by means of a technical edacdtion are compelled to avail themselves of the educational facilities of other towns, while those whose means will lot permit of this have to plod on as best they can, filled with life-long regrets at the want of en- terpriee on the part of our public men. Time was when , Warrington possessed such an institution as Mr. Diggle I suggested, but it seems as if some of its students, having risen to fame, were too much absorbed with their own arm- CeB9 to think of extending a helping band to others. How sad it is to see our young reel going read over football, and epending their evenings at street cornere blinding themselves with tobacco smoke, just because no nobler w eye of spend- ing their time are provided. Warringtfn is woefully be- hind the timer' in matters tending to develope the better +panties of its inhabitants, and it ii to be hoped an effort towards improvement in this direction will signalise this Jubilee year. That it is urgently wanted no one will deny. Bet to ask for intellecttail fond, and to get the promise of fireworks, is worse than asking for bread and getting a stone. There is some suharance in A stone, but what in the world is there in fireworks? Depend upon it, working-men want no fireworks, and what is more, they want no procession. /do doubt lawyers and parsons would cut nice figures in a street 'P-otacle, with their gowns and, .liege cape, but whet about working•man, whose only dress is moleskin. If there is to be anything at all, let it be sen- sible, and somethin,‘ that will tend to elevate all who take / have paid. the most thonghful suggestion part In it. As that has yet been made was that of a Mechanics' Institute, I and I for one trust it will receive cermideration by the large committee appointed to take the celebration in hand. REMEMBER DIGGLE. Warrington, March 9, 1887.

He accuses m-i of bavisg written a "peevish and discourteous letter, in every line of which there lurks a pa!pable secretion of venous," and than after this 'talent and somewhat coarse ebullition of temper, he protests that he dnee not wish to be hash with me. In conclusion, let me say that if Alderman Harrison had guided his conduct by a wise discretion, instead of allowing be vanity to control his better Fidgment, he would not have assumed a position which is not his, neithe, would he (to quote hie *VIII words) have" rush.] in ti print with a silly letter, in every line of which, in addition to its abstirdity, there lurks a palpable secretion of venom, too feeble and puerile to sting, yet lackinEr not the quality, under the peculiar circumstances, to be offensive."—Yours tr

THOUGHTS ON TWO LEO ['MIEN AND MR. G 4NDY.

Sir,—l accept Mr. Gandy's letter ss he ng the candid ex- pression of his honest opinions. I hope he will accord to me the same courtesy. lam sorry to see him get into a rage. In this heated state he forgets that I merely men- tioned the statements of others, and askA some questions. And lam still in this inquisitive mood. Does Mr. Gaudy and his like believe that GA through Moses and the Bible tells us that He created us and all existing things in six days—and, to make this statement still more definite, added the words, so often repeated, and there was evening, and there was morning ?" Does he and thee know that this statement of Moses is flatly contradicted by the fasts of geolyogv.? Is it not true that he and such as he are guilty of the illogical impiety of trying te tinker the Word of God so as to make it "Naar,/ with the revelations if science," when they deny that when God said six days lie means it, and not some hid-finite " periods " as they say He meant? And if the six days are periods of unknown length, how eloes Mr. Gandy arrive at his Sabbath ? Must not that be a period also, and ono in all probability not yet arrived?

Are we to infer that Messrs. Gandy and Co. know the Divine Author's meaning better than He knew it er could express it Himself ? and has it reqaired the lapse of all these desolate centuries, and the appearance of such lumin- aries as Dawson, Gandy, it Co., to expound this text to uo, and to teach us that the All Wire meant one thing when-He said another? Cannot these poor p-ople see that to mutilate and stultify an author is not the best way to defend him from his critics? Would it be possible to convince them that to pull down the walls of their fortress in order to pelt the enemy with the debris is not to be resorted to except in the Msence of better ammunition? Can believers in Reve- lation do otherwise than accept this text as it was given by its Divine Author literally without mutilation or alterm ties? Is it not a suspicious circumstance that the neces- sity for such impious and illogical tampering with the I text has only arisen since it became possible to read it I by the light of modern science Does Mr. Gandy think Hugh Miller, who, poor fellow, found refuge in suicide from the difficulties of recouciling the nedoubted facts of his lenience with the statements of Mmes,—does he think him to be an authoriry on evolut:on as it is to day? Then as the facts of geology and archmtlegy utterly con- fate the statement of Moses—so neither Mr. Gand• nor any ether mortal must be permitted to pare and shape them ; till they do so, can any remelting being do otherwise than accept the facts even if he must discard the statement? So I come to the object of my pre•ions letter, and ask: Is it right to continue to teach the statements in our Sunday Schools, asd to give the lie direct in the day schools by teaching the facts? What but confusion of ideas aids disbelief in the better parts of the Bible can be looked fir if a hey is told in the Sunday School that six days were sufficient for Creation, and finds in the week that six mil- lions are not enough ? Can the teaching of one truth des- troy another Is it likely that any subsequent d ircove, ies of science will in any way lessee the beauty sod motility of the iejunction to " Do unto others ao ye would they they should do unto you "? Then if true religion and , morality will not suffer by the discovery and promulgation of scientific truth,but only bibliolatry,who will be the worse though they be proclaimed from the hottse.tops ? JOHN PEERS. Penketh, 14th March, 1887.

THE INFLUENCE OF MACHINERY ON THE PROSPERITY OF THE PEOPLE Sir,—You have been kind enough to allow a little of your space for the consideration of a subject near akin to the lecture yon report under the above heading, and giver by Mr. Thomas Morris. Will you be kind enough to continue your favour, so that I and Mr. Gandy may have another tilt at this, second to none as the most burning question of the day ? lam not prepared to fall down, as Mr. Morris and Mr. Gandy seem inclined to, and worship this Moloch of the nineteenth century—machinery; nor yet am I prepared to eche the burning words Mr. Ruskin has just delivered him- self of respecting the Ambleside railway scheme; but this .1 atn sure of, that unless steam and machinery are btought more within the control, and rendered more subject to man and his necessities, the human family will suffer accord- ingly. I fear that the mistake Mr. Morris makes is one common to most superficial readers, that is. of failing to recognise the whole of the circumstances influencing society at given periods, or dates. A hundred years ago, the lot of the com- mon labourer was one of comparative happiness; he might have been ignorant, his borne might have been destitute of the commonest necessaries of to-day. He, his wife, and his children might, nay did, work from early morn till dewy eve. All the same, their misery was not made more acute by contact will the ether extreme; that is, the refined and leLured luxury of to-day. I put a plain question to our two friends, and one admitting at a plain answer : Are the environmencs of present day society producing satisfactory results?

Robert Owen taught that " man was the creature of cir- cumstances." For this he was declaimed against from platform, pulpit, and press. It was argued that man was the creator of the circumstances that moulded his fate. As is usual, the truth lies between the two, and in the social revolt now going on we find a steady determination on the part of labour to bring the force of will power to bear upon mere inert matter. In other words, aimless discontent ie struggling to formulate a basis upon which the social life of the people may be rendered happier, by bringing into sub- jection, the wild and selfish invendvenees nature hoe en- dowed man with. It has always been beyond my compre- hension haw any man could urge the superior vlane of any one man's labour to that of another. The scavenge! who mechanically carries out the behests of the sanitary laws, does more for toe comfort of min than a thousand great captains; yet what is the lot of each? to one is allotted a life of painful and degrading drudgery, and to the other a nation's honour. So it is with the man of inventive genius. The brain developes, and the muscle carries out, the two together making the complete whole. The secret of our trouble is, that medern life is essentially one of shams. Everything is artificial, and so we have cores to have artificial wants, which in their turn have brought about a want that is real in its inten.ity, and causes in London riotous meetings in Trafalgar Square, and demonstrations anything but palatable o the worshippers In St. Paul's; a want that wrecks whole towns, as at Char- lerio ; and most painful of all leads to the gallows men wild with anguish, as at Chicago. At the commencement of this epoch of machinery we had riots, as Mr. Morris notices' caused by a not unreasonable or unjustifiable dread of machinery. Men, hungering for their rights, combined to agitate for the charters of their man- hood; hence we had the Chartists, a high and pure-toned band of men. These found themselves suddenly face to face with mechanical problems which they weie unable to solve. A stern and an unbending master had quite unexpectedly come amongst them, and threatened to displace them. What is the sequel which we in after days have lived to sea? This, that we have huge and unwieldy masses of people living huddled together in town and city. " Where faster and faster our iron master The thing we =we, for ever drives, Bids us grind treasure and fashion pleasure For other hopes ant other lives " The "rest and be thankful" tone that pervades the teach- ings of Mr. Morris and Mr. Gandy, makes one ask, with Mr. F. Harrison," Is the universal use of a mechanical process per se, a great gain to civilisation, an unmixed gain—a gain without dangers or drawbacks?" I maintain that it is not • machinery cannot be accepted as the instrument whereby ; we hope to realise our ideals of a higher, socid, and moral life. Most of your readers will have at their finger ends a long string of appliances, all destined to do good service to humanity. But is this good of se unmixed a character that we used not pause ? Take Mr. Morris's instance of the shoe trade. Have we better shoes than our grandfathere had? Do we find them cheaper, taking durability into account ? Certainly not; they are considerably dearer, and from a hygienic point of view vastly more injurious. Would it not be better then to rase the shoe factory to the ground, and multiply indefioitely the number of lapstones in the laud, and agree once more that there is "nothing like leather." Mr. Morris tells us that "machinery had, must, and ever would gain the mastery over manual labour." What a sorrowful confession for a "thinking man " to make! shall it be said that the resources of civilisation are exhausted when we speak of the mechanical crisis throngh which we are passing? Surely not; I for one refuse to believe that we are so stupified with smoke, and stunned with steam whistles, that we must fold our arms, and allow the machine to rush with us violently down a Steep place, like the herd of swine. I power, earH own that the machine le, as an agent, and by Its very a by its scientific precision. the muter over manna labour, but what then? When rpferring to the machine, and is the labour question, several things have to be considered, amongst which are—Are the things made needed? Such for instance as armour plates, war ships, and lot cannons. Again, is Mr. Morris sati,fied that the two elements, labour and capital, co-operate fairly to bring about the most desirable results ? Take a supposed cage: number of capitalists throw together their mot,ey and start a big concern. They appoint one another to fall the van. Owl posts, as to management, dm., these posts, of course

div.head: EX A.MINER. SATURDAY. MARCTI 19, 1887.
div.p: THE EX A.MINER. SATURDAY. MARCTI 19, 1887.

carrying with there good salaries. Where does the mutual Interest come in between these capitalists and the laboorer—the one receiving interest on money invested, with profit, if any, besides a fixed salary, and the other, the labourer,doemed to see his wage, not salary, at the mercy of every wild inrush of cipital tempted by the facilities afforded by the Limited Liability Act? It has been said truly that" cur present type tit society is in many respects one of the meet horrible that has ever existed In the world's history—boundless luxury and self-indulgence at one end of the scale and at the other a condition of life as cruel as that of a Roman slave, and more degraded than that of a South Sea Islander."

Look carefully at our modern eystens of production, dating from the lattPr half of the last century. What is it? In- creased antagonism as the years rol! on. The basis is un- mend, and harmony impossible. It leads to the extremes of wealth aed poverte—.o vast accumulations in the handy of the few, and to the degradation •f the toiling rnillione The imstructemts of labour machinery are but the results of the accumulated labours of all past ages, the outcome of thought, and the results of the highest intelligence. The present generation has but a life interest in them ; as we took them from the past, so they must goon to the future. I are not mistaking the tenoar of Mr. Morris's paper I noticed that it was a simple adulation of machinery, the writer not stopping to consider whether the capitalist or the labourer received, as years rolled on, their rightful share of its benefits. But is it not time that we did something more than follow blindly the machine mania with which people seem to be possessed ? In a report just issued by Govern- ment we t3r.d that in bulk our trade .has suffered no depree- , siert ; year by year it has increased, but the numbor of ' labourers has decreased. This statement should 'flake us us pleas. Carpenter, in his work on " Machinery," states that 1817 the population was 29,250,000. the number of workers 5.200000, and the prnductive powers of machinery was equal to the labour of 200,000,000 men. In 1840 the population was 26,500,000, the number of workers 6,800.000, and the productive power of machinery was equal to 600,000,000. From I°4o to 1878 the productive power of mactnnory had again doubled, being equal to the labour of 1,200,000,000 of wen. Now I ask ongnt all this power to be in the hands of individuals ? Oueht it to be left under the control and discretion of a few ? Certainly net. So far as our inventions double and treble the power of the rich, land double arid treble the helplessness et the poor, no far do those gre it materi +I appliances of life directly tend to lower civilisation, retard it, d stort, and deprave it. •• All e,vlll-ing arts we boast. What does the vaunted progress cost ? Alai for ra-th„ if this great gain Have its foundations laid in oat,— ' Fain of the poor who •,uffer still. Lot She world brighten as it will." COLIN CLOUT.

div.head: EPIDEMIC OF MEASLES.
div.p: EPIDEMIC OF MEASLES.

We regret to learn from Dr. Gornall, the Medical Officer of Health for Warrington, that there has been a serious extension' of measles during the last ten days. Since Monday, the 7th inst., there have been over 100 notifications by medical men. A more accurate state of affairs is arrived at by con- sulting the school registers. Dr. Gornall has ascer- tained, as to three schools where the disease is most prevalent, that the number on the registers is 1,029, and that the aumber absent from measles is 220. In any stage of a measles epidemic it is well known that personal communication is the princi- pal method of extension. This is promoted by chil- dren attending school in the early stage of the disease (which is frequently undistinguishable), and by returning to school before they " cease to , become infective. The only method at the pre. sent time of arresting its progress is by closing the schools in question. Dr. Gornall recommends this course to be taken, and it will of course be done. It is an extreme step, as closing schools prejudicially affects the examination; but an epidemic of this magnitude requires prompt and effective treatment.

PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY. As will be seen from the report of the business, for the past year, this gigantic society continues to make extraordinary progress. • The expenditure is effected with due regard for economy; in the or- dinary branch the rate was little more than ten per cent on the premium income; while in the indus- trial branch there is a slight reduction in the rate of expenditure. It is exceedingly satisfactory to find on turning to the list of assets that they are of a really solid kind. The members of some societies have little more to depend on than the personal stability of the directors ;' but the assets of the Prudential include over one million sterling in 3 pei cent consols, considerably over a million in freehold ground rents, &c., and something like a million and a half on loans in municipal and other rates, besides Bank of England stock, railway debentures, &c. Turning to the figures we find that the assurance funds have been increased during the year by the sum of £l,l22,os4—namely, the ordinary branch £319,496, and the industrial branch £802,558. The total assets of the company amount to ,X 6,811,954. In the ordinary branch the number of policies issued during the year was £25,567, assuring the sum of .£2,715,429, and producing a new annual premium income of £125,604. The premiums of the year were £396,940, being an increase of £93,665 over the year 1885. The claims of the year amounted to £135,361. The number of deaths was 944, and 40 endowment assurances matured. The rate of expenditure of the branch was little more than 10 per cent. on the premium income. The number of policies in force was 85,089. In the in- dustrial branch the premiums received during the year were £2,911,295, being all increase 0f.£116,773. The claims of the year amounted to £1,123,428. The number of deaths was 135,851. The rate of ex- penditure of the branch shows a slight reduction. The number of policies in force, including 58,099 free policies, was 7,111,828. The quinquennial re- port for the period ending December al, 1886, shows that in the ordinary branch the annual pre- mium income has increased from £142,732 to £407,360. The assurance fund has grown from £744,583 to £1,764,600. in the industrial branch the annual premium income has increased from £2,051,024 to £3,065,551, ard the assurance fund has grown from £1,721,493 to £4,937,003, while the total assets of the company have grown from £2,580,002 to £6,811,954, Win', an ' increase of £4,231,952 in the five years under inspection. The officers of the company in this district are Mr. T. Rowland, 55, Bouverie-street, Chester, Superinten dent; Mr. J. Jephcot, 29, Waterloo-road, Ituncorn, Assistant-Superintendent; and Mr. E. Weighill, 6, Cambrian View, Chester, Assistant Superintendent. _

MR. RIGBY ON DANY FIiIICATION. At the last meeting of the London Farmers' Club, Mr. Rigby, well known in this district as the secretary of the Roy-al North Lancashire and Manchester and Liverpool Agricultural Society, read an able paper on Dairy Educa- tion. After alluding to the agencies which facilitated the progress of education in the details of the diary, he proceeded :—I may be thought to have assumed the case of defective knowledge or defective practice in dairying without justification. I have an honest belief that four- fifths and more of both dairymen and dairymaids do their best to make good and superior quality of both butter and cheese, and they are not culpable when they fail. Nearly all dairy workers are personally interested in suc- cess, and most of them, therefore, will try to succeed. As a fact, patient and constant labour is given ungrudg- ingly to cheese and butter making in farm houses, and when a young mother with two or three young children round her knees presides at the cheese-tub with ten or twelve cheeses under press that rufuse to dry, and an extra staff of labourers to feed, as is often the case in harvest time in Cheshire, she &serves more consideration than these sharp reflections carry. There is a failure—partial failure at least is ' acknowledged—and failure that is a great loss bith to tenants and to landlords and the pros- perity of the country. Some butter fetches id. per lb. more than others, some 2d., and even 3d. Some cheese (whole-milk cheese and cream-butter are being com- pared) will not sell for so much as other by 58., 10s., or even 20s. per cwt., and is more difficult of sale at this reduction. Yet the milk was all of similar quality. The, interest we are discussing is not a little one or of small value. There are 97,000 calving cows and heifers in Cheshire alone. Assume that one-third of their number are kept to supply milk only, and that the milk of 65,000 is made into butter and cheese; estimate it all as cheese at 3 cwts. per cow to trace out its value, the result is 9,750 tons, which, if sold at 50s. per cwt, equals £487,500; at 60s. per cwt. it equals £585,000. It is considered a fair and favourable thing to say that one - fourth of Cheshire - made cheese sells at the highest price of the year, one- half at a medium, and one-fourth at the lowest average price, these three qualities being distant each about be. per cwt. from the other. It will follow, therefore, that if the maximum price be 50s. per cwt., the loss from reduction Of quality will be 4.875 tons at £6, and 2,434 at £lO per ton, or a total of £48,750! Or, to bring it into practical personal application—a farm of 40 cows, making 3 cwts. of cheese per cow, would lose £3O if made of only medium quality, and £6O if of lowest average quality, the labour in both cases being the same, and the satisfaction with results much less. The losses from deficient quality run sometimes up to 10s. per cwt. The inference to be drawn is, that improvement is pos- sible all round; that there is a higher stave than the highest rung in the ladder yet scaled; that great im- provement in dairying is further possible. More is possible on some farms than others. Improvement in quality—better prices, more satisfaction with work done by dairymaids, and with produce purchased by con- sumers,

BAND OF HOPE MEETING. On Wednesday evening a public meeting of the Primitive Methodist Band of Hope was held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, presided over by Mr. illiam Ringrose, of 1:won. The following humorous dialogues were given, together with recitations and songs by the choir, assisted by friends :—" The landlord in a fix," "Apartments to let,'" and "Annie and Emma." Tne latter was so well rendered that the piece was re-demanded by the audience. TEMPERANCE MErritro —& public meeting of the Church of England Temperance Society was held in the Town Hall, Frodsbam, on Monday evening, presided over by the vicar, the Rev. H. B. Blogg. The Chairman spoke of the great importance of the temperance work, and the Rev. A. P. Reynolds, of Kingsley, compared the teetotalism of the pre- sent time with what it was some years agq. Mr. Clarke Aspinall, of Liverpool, dwelt on local option, and of the necessity of putting the right temperance men forward as magistrates, for the protection and benefit of the poorer classes.

Rev A P Reynolds; and 10, Node'', Rey It R Whitehead; making a total of 175. The Bishop addressed the candidates in a very kind and sympathetic manner. The Rev H B Blogg, vicar of Frodsham, acted as chaplain to the Bishop during the service. Frodshatn, on Friday evening, Mr. Alfred Thomas in the chair, the accounts from Mr. Timmins, amounting to £22 3s 6d, for alleged detention of his plant at the Newton Trial Wells, was again produced, when it was resolved that as the Committee had incurred no lia- bility they could only confirm their previous resolution- A report was read from the surveyor to the trustees of the late Major Bitchen with reference to the overflow of water at the Trial Wells, and it was resolved that the Committee were not responsible for anything further in this matter, the Committee having done all they wrre asked to de under the agreement. An account was sebmitted from Mr. John Littler for £l3 183 5d for drainage connections to main sewer at Overton, which was submitted to the Authority for payment. Plans were produced from Messrs Linaker and Davies fer a new house to be erected in Church-street, Frodsham, for Mr. George Sharrock, the same having been found to comply with the building bye-laws and were re- commended to the Authority for approval.

The usual fortnightly meeting of this body was held on Tuesday afternoon at Dutton Workhouse. Lieutenant. Colonel Ashton presided, sod there were also present Mr. Weir (vice-chairman), the Revs. J. div.head: WIDNES WESLEYAN METHODIST CIRCUIT.
div.p: WIDNES WESLEYAN METHODIST CIRCUIT.

The quarterly meeting in connection with the Widnes Wesleyan Methodist Circuit, was held on Monday, at Lacey- street School. The local preachers met at half-past two, brethren being present from all parts of the circuit, and at five o'clock tea was provided by Mr. and Mrs. William Sadler. The repast was an exceedingly good one, and the manner in which it wee served added much to its attractiveness, the tables being taste- fully adorned with choice plants and flowers. There were about seventy persons present at tea, including many ladies from all parts of the circuit A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. and Mrs. William Sadler, on the motion of ' the Stewards.—The Rev. R. Burdon presided over the sub- sequent meetinE„ and reported a slight increase of members on the year. The stewards' accounts showed that they had a balance in hand. The Rev. J Bryant presented the annual returns of the Sunday schools in the circuit, showing 1885 scholars an 4 193 teachers, as against 1663 and 180 last year, an increase of 222 and 13 respectively. The libraries at the schools contained 2,244 books against 1,107 in 1885, an increase of 1,137, while the number of readers has gone tm from 214 to 332. Sanction was given to the friends at li'arnworth to go on with their scheme for the erection of a Sunday school and classrooms, estimated to cost about £5OO, a large portion of which sum is already in hand or premised, and a baz ler la aid of the project is to be held in May. The Revs. R. Burdon and James Bryant were heartily thanked for their past services, and received and accepted an unanimous invitotion to labour in the circuit 'anther year.

div.p: WIDN.E4 SCHOOL BOARD.

- - The monthly meeting was held on Tueoday, at the offices, Victoria-road. Mr. T. S. Timmis presided, and there were present the Rev. Dean Finegan, the Revs. Father Clarke and G. Bond. Messrs. Bradshaw. Davis, Deacon, Imisoo, Heves, Wareing, and Dr. O'Keeffe, with Mr. Denby (clerk).

div.head: DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTER.
div.p: DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTER.

This committee reported that during February there were 170 applications for payment of fees, and t6s'y were recom- mended to be paid in 154 cases. There were 335 persons before the committee for contravention of the Education Act, atad 30 were convicted by the macistrates. Two chil- dren were committed to the industrial school. It was recommended that on the completion of 10 years' service the salary of attendance officer H. Davies be increased ac- cording to the scale of the Board, the increase to commence April Ist, 1887.—The minutes were passed on the proposi- tion of Mr. H. Wade Deacon. THE PROPOSED INCREASE OF FEES.

The School Management Committee recommended that the following reasons for increasing the school fees be for- warded to the Education Department in reply to their m- quiry dated February 3rd, 1887:—" 1. That when the scale of fees payable in the Board schools was sanctioned by the Education Department there teas no seventh standard in existnee. 2. That the requirements of the present seventh standard are far in excess of anything which the Code re- quired when the Board's scale of fees were fixed, and con- sequently demand more teaching staff. 3. lhat the class of children in standard seven as a class are beet able to pay.— , In moving the adoption of the recommendation, Dean Fine- , gat' remarked that there could be no discussion as to whether the fees should be raised or not. They had siinply to give the reasons wh,ch had induced the committee to re- commend, and the Beard to sanction, the increase.—Tho Chairman said he had no hesitation in recommending the Board to adopt the reply. Be thought the reasons fair and satisfactory.—Mr. Deacon objected to the increase of fees, , and therefore he objected to those or any reasons.—Mr. . Hayes seconded the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Davis , objected, because he thought thetetatements made were not reasons. The sentence numbered three was a libel upon the poorer classes, and in effect said they wore less intelli- gent and less industrious than the children of the better to do. Therefore be considered that as a reason it was quite unworthy of the Management Committee. He objected to the whole thing.—Mr.Beyes replied that the reasons given were simply facts within the knowledge of the School Man- &gement Committee.—The Rev. G. Bond said the committee judged from the list of children in the class prepared for them by Mr. Denial', and the number being small that they were quite justified in proposing the increased fee.—The Chairman remarked that he was quite sure this answer had been carefully prepared, and the throe words in italics i would enable him to vote for t. Though there were some who could not pay, he believed that "as a class" it was true.—Mr. Wareing objected to the advance of fees, but they had to give reasons for that course, and probably these were as good reasons as any that could be sent.—Dean Fine- gan said there might be other reasons, and good ones too, but as far as his memory would carry him these were the reasons brought forward by the committee Rhea they asked the Board to accept the change, and for these reasons the Board sanctioned the change. He regretted that he bad to object to the reniarks of a per- son of the standing of Mr. Davis when he said it was un- worthy of the committee. It was a strong expression to use of a committee who bad acted, as the chairman con- sidered, prudently and conscientiously, and to ihow that they had done nothing at random they obtained the names of the children who are in the 7th standard, and they would find that many of these scholars were children of the better class shopkeeper or builder in the district. As a class there were more children in the 7th standard than in. any other standard. He did not think the committee had ever done anything unworthy of gentlemen, and he asked Mr. Davis to study his words carefally, because the committee were net in the habit of hearing sag: words addressed to them. They were not Parliamentary, and he regretted that the chairman, who ought to protect them, had not called attention to the words.—The Chairman said he 'did think the words were rather strong, but he did not believe that Mr. Davis wished to imply that the course was unworthy ef gentlemen.—Mr. Davis : Can I speak again, Mr. Chair- man ?—The Chairman : No ; you can withdraw the words if you like.—Mr. Davis did not take this course, and the reply was adopted by ten votes to one, only Mr. Davis voting against.

The School Manageotent Committee reported that they /lad it a room in the Simm's Cross Board School to Mrs.
Thompson, a certificated teacher of Kindergarten classes, io which to hold classes for teachers.
A COMPLAINT.

The committee also reported that they bad fully inves- tigated the charges brought by Mrs James Bennett, of 21, Frederick-street (in a letter to the chairman of the Board) against the teachers in the senior girl's department of the Bimm's Cross Schools, and consider that the case was one not calling for their interference.

div.p: A 11IIMOLIR.

Mr. Wareing asked "Whether the rumour is true which Is current in the town that the School Management Com- mittee have promised to recommend to the Board that the former allowance of 25 per cent of the drawing grant earned in the schools, hitherto paid by the Board, is to be re-insta- ted on the Board's scale of salaries, and if so, when such increase is to be recommended."—Dean Finegan, after a few humorous remarks on the difficulty of understanding the question, said that for reasons that appaared wise the committee had had the subject before them as to when such increase was to be recommended ; he thought they had better wait until they got the grant betore they divided it.

NOTICE IS HER,EBY GIVEN, that at a Meeting of the Local Authority of the Borongh of Warrington. held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday, the Six. eenth day of March, 1887. the said Local Authority lot the purpose 01 preventing the introduction of Swine Fever, made the Regulatioas following, that is to say :- 1. These Regulations shall commence and take effect from and immediately after the Twepty-second day of March instant, and shall continue in for a until the Eighteenth day ot April next, unless Eo, mar revtked or altered by the Local Authority of the Borough of Warrington. 2. No swine shall be moved into the Borough of Warring- ton from the district of any other Loral Authority un- less a Movement Licence be flret obtained, which shall only be granted on a declaration being made by the Owner or his Agent ti the L.llowing effent:— (1) That such swine has not bens elsewhere than on the farm or lands from which the movement is to be made during 28 days immediately preceding the date of the applisation for the license. . (2) That swine fever has not existed on such farm or lands, or on any adjoining farm or lands. (3) That such swine has not been exptse,i in any market, fair, exhibitien, or public sale, within the said 28 days. The foregoing regulations shall not re, frict the movement of swine by railway through the Borough of Warrington. Dated this Seveiteenth day of starch 1881. WM. KY. BROOK, Town Clerk. N.B.—Licenses may be obtained from Inspector Nor nan, at the Town Hall, who will also supply forms of declaration above mentioned.

Whereas it appears to us the undersigned, three of Her Majesty's Justices of the Peace for the Gounty of Chester, act- ing in and for the Division of Runcorn, in the std County, within which Division and County the folio. ing Townships, namely :—Aston Grange, Aston-bv-suttun, Clifton, Halton, Norton, Runcorn, Stockham, Button, and Weston, are situate. and being the Local Authority for the said Division. as defiaed by " The Dogs Act, 1871," in Petty Sessions assembled at the usual place of meeting, this 141 h day of March, 1887, at the Petty Sessional Court House in Runcorn. In the said Division and County, that there is cause to surpeo,. and reasonable ground for believing that CANINE MADNESS is prevalent 1 within the Division of Runcorn aforesaid: Now we. therefore, by virtue and in pursuance of the statutes in this behalf, and of all other powers and authorities there- unto enabling us, hereby order and direct all Ow ers of Dogs, or persons having Dogs, within the befire-mentioned town- ships, to keep such Dogs confined nr under proper personal control, and not to suffer the same to be at large, except when securely muzzled. And any Dog not being under such control or muzzled as aforesaid, or found straying in any sit eet or highway may be, and we hereby authorise the same to be detained, sold, or destroyed. in pursuance of the said Act. And this our order shall take effect and remain in force from the day of the date hereof, until the first day of May now next ensuing. Any person acting in contravention of the above order will subject himself to a penalty oi Twenty Shillings for each offeace. Given under our hands and seals this Fourteenth day of March, 1887, at Riumorn, in the said Division and County. . JOHN BRUNDRIT 411 ALFRED THOMAS 411 G. L. DAVIES

It was doubtful whether greaterinjustice was being perpetrated anywhere, perhaps \ et 'fret 'unwittingly, but knowingly now, than in the Cheshire salt district. The land lying over salt beds was owned by a great number of persons, very few of whom pumped brine. The streams of brine in their way to the pumping centres passed over the salt underlying the, property of the non-pumpers, and in passing away dissolved' a portion of the salt and carried it away. In consequence the surface smk and the houses and other pro- perty on it were seriously damaged. The non- pumper had his salt taken, and his surface property damaged- at the same time. As water was used to-mine the salt, and as no one could say which par- ticular pumper did an especial injury, it was impossible as the law stood, to obtain ipompensarion. RUNCORN UNION.—CONTRACTS for PROVISIONS and SUPPLIES for the half-year ending 29th September, 1887.—The GUARDIAN(' of the ,0011 of the RUNCORN UNION are desirous uf receiving TENDERS from parties willing to CONTRACT for the supply of New Milk, Buttermilk, Fresh Butter and Fresh Eggs (for Twelve Months), Flour. Oat- meal, Groceries, Peas, Cheese, Salt Butter ; Cod Liver and Paraffin Oil; Quinine; good Beef, to consist of vein and brisket pieces, the price to include about 301198. per week of the best butcher's meat for the officers, and sides of IMutton; Best Brand (lets) American or English Bacon; Pota- toes; Wheat Straw; Drapers, and Clothing; Men's, Women's, Boys' and Girls' Shoes, of various sizes, as per samples to be seen at the Workhouse, Dutton; House Coal (colliery to be named); good Deal Coffins, specifying size, and Including plate with name, age and date of death, to be de- livered in the Union when. and where required ; Cart- fog at per mile, and Funerals at per funeral. Parties tendering for the supply of the above-mentioned goods will be required to deliver the same at the Workhouse, free of cost to the Guardians, how and when required. Tenders to be accompanied with samples (except drapery goods) as far as practicable. The Guardians do not bind themselves to ac- cept the lowest or any tender. Persons desirous of tendering must apply by letter to my office, in Frodsham, for a printed Form of Tender (and none other csn be entertained), where a schedule of the various articles requlred and further particulars may beobtained. Sealed Tenders, addressed to the Guardians, to be forwasded to the Clerk's office, Frodsham. on or before Monday, the 28th day of March, 1887, endorsed "Tender for ." The tenders will be opened and considered at a raellting of the Guardians to be held in the Board Room, Dutton, on the 29th March, 1887, at Two p.m. Parties whose tenders are accepted must enter into a written contract, and be prepared to enter into a bond with two sureties, if re- quired by the Guardians. By order of the Board, H. LINAKER. Frodsham, Ist March, 1887. Clerk to the Guardians.

The body of a man named Quayle was found on the rail- way at Walton, on Friday, terribly mutilated, the arms and legs being levered. At a conference on Friday of Airdrie and Slarnannan coal masters and men, held in Glasgow, a settlement of the dis- pute was arranged. Lord Rosebery has consented to be the Liberal candidate for Glasgow University en Professor Lushington's retire- ment next November. It is reported that Mr. William M'Arthur is to be asked to contest the seat rendered vacant by the resignation of Mr. Borlase, M.P., who retiree through ill-health. At a meeting of millers held in London, on Friday, it was resolved to call upon the National Association to institute an inquiry into the desirability of an import duty on foreign flour. The Central News understands that Sir William Hart Dyke will accede to the wish of Welsh members that the Welsh language shall be included among the class subjects In article fifteen of the Education Code. EARTHQUAKE IN CUBA. Diner YORK, Flamm—lntelligence from Cuba announces that a slight earthquake. shock was felt at Quemades yes- terday. A shock was also felt at Charleston, but no damage is reported. FIRE IN AMERICA.-15 LIVES LOST. NEW YORK, FRIDAY Arrnstrioosr.—The damage caused by the fire at the Richmond Hotel, Buffalo, is estimated at three hundred thousand dollars. About fifteen lives were. boat, and a large number of people were injured. LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at fear o'clock. The Earl of ONsLow, replying to the Earl of HarrowbY, said the Government desired that the forthcoming Colonial Conference should be representative in its character, and representatives from all the Crown Colonies bad been in- vited, in addition to those of the self-governing colonies. The Home shortly afterwards adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at 4 o'clock NOTICE, &C.—Sir H. lIOSCDE gave notice that on an early day be should draw attention to the subject of opening museums on Sundays.—The IRISH SECRETARY, replying to Mr. Chance, declined to lay on the table a copy of Judge O'Brien's charge to Antrim Grand Jury after the Belfast riote.—The Wen SECRETARY, replying to Mr. McCartney, said the orders given to the police in Ireland were confi- dential and could not be communicated to the House. TB ARREST OF FATHER BELLER —Mr. DILLost asked for and obtained leave to move the adjournment of the House in order to call attention to the arrest of the Rev. T. Keller, at Youghall, under a warrant of Judge Boyd for contempt. He insisted that compelling Father Keller to attend the Binkruptcy Court and give information against one of his flock was an outrage.—Mr. Bacroure said that nothing but ordinary steps to carry out the law had taken place as regarded the arrest of Father Keller. The laws must be obeyed. The ordems of the court most be carried out, and both would be done if agitators gave up exciting people to resist that law.—Mr. PICTON and Mr. ARTHUR O'CONNOR condemned the speech of the Irish Secretary.— Mr. JACOB BRIGHT asked for further information as to the death of Hanlon.—Mr Slant said the matter was now being legally investigated, and therefore it would nJt be right to enter into details.—The di.cussion was continued by Messrs. Chance, Ellis, Conybeare, O'Doberty, J. B. Roberts, Dr. Tanner, and O'Brien' each condemning the action of the Irish police in charging unarmed people with fixed , bayonets. Darr =rule. j
